articles.title: StuckInProfit, AFAZ partner on Africa–Azerbaijan enterprise development pilot - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African SME-focused business education company StuckInProfit has partnered with the Africa–Azerbaijan Cooperation (AFAZ) to launch a three-week virtual professional and enterprise development programme, to kick off in November.
The StuckInProfit × AFAZ Professional & Enterprise Development Programme 2026 will see participants coached by a network of AFAZ instructors across 11 areas, including project presentation, emotional intelligence, leadership, virtual collaboration, time management, finance for non-finance professionals, entrepreneurship, critical thinking, creativity and intercultural communication.
The programme’s instructors are drawn largely from Azerbaijan’s academic, corporate and development sectors. They include ADA University senior instructor Aygün Mammadova, international development specialist Nadir Guluzade, former Ministry of Economy official Natig Madatov, and Hokuma Karimova, director of public relations and corporate communications at Nar (Azerfon).
Beyond the pilot, the partners say the longer-term goal is to build practical bridges between African entrepreneurs, SMEs and professional talent and international ecosystems through education, capacity development and market knowledge.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (September 30, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (September 30, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for September 30, 2026.
YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.
Funding news
Arivihan raises $10M
Arivihan, an AI-powered learning platform for school students, has raised $10 million in a Series A round co-led by existing investors Accel and Prosus Ventures, along with another $200,000 from GSF angel investors. The latest funding takes the Indore-based startup’s total capital raised to more than $15 million. Founded by IIT Roorkee alumni Ritesh Singh Chandel and Sonu Kumar, along with maths educator Rushabh Kothari, Arivihan combines interactive video lessons, instant doubt-solving and AI-generated study plans that adapt to students’ performance.
EDT raises $2.4M Pre-Series A led by Sauce, expands into beauty-tech with SUKI
EDT, a design and technology brand focused on everyday appliances, has raised $2.4 million in an oversubscribed Pre-Series A round led by existing investor Sauce, with existing angels also increasing their investments.
The round drew new investors, including Alteria Capital, Raul Rai of Nicobar, Shibam Das and Arindam Paul of Atomberg, Ajith Pai of Delhivery, and Anushree Tainwala of Samsonite.
EDT will use the fresh capital to build inventory ahead of the festive season across channels, launch new products, and strengthen its growth, supply chain, brand and product teams.
The fundraise comes as EDT expands beyond kitchen appliances to build a broader consumer design and technology platform spanning home, kitchen and beauty-tech. As part of this expansion, the company has launched SUKI, a new beauty-tech and personal care brand.
Prodoc AI raises seed funding
Bengaluru-based healthcare AI company Prodoc AI has raised an undisclosed amount in a seed funding round led by Dr A Velumani Family Office. The round also saw participation from Dr Kunal Shet and Parth D Bhasin, both existing users of Prodoc AI’s platform who invested in the company.
Prodoc AI is building a Patient Journey OS to address the fragmentation across hospital technology systems. Hospitals typically use multiple standalone platforms for functions such as hospital information systems, electronic medical records, customer relationship management, billing, telephony and diagnostics. Prodoc AI’s software sits across these existing systems, creating an intelligence layer that brings patient context together and coordinates workflows without requiring hospitals to replace their existing infrastructure.
The company plans to use the fresh capital to advance its Agentic AI capabilities, expand its system integrations and develop AI agents for complex hospital workflows across care coordination, patient engagement, operations and revenue management.
Other news
Chiratae appoints Keshav R Murugesh to Global Advisory Board
Chiratae has appointed Keshav R. Murugesh to its Global Advisory Board as the venture capital firm marks 20 years of backing India’s entrepreneurial ecosystem.
Murugesh brings more than three decades of experience in building, transforming and scaling global technology and business services companies. In his new role, he will advise Chiratae on strategy, governance, talent and scaling high-growth startups into enduring global businesses.
He currently serves as Special Advisor to the Group CEO and is a member of Capgemini's Group Executive Committee. Murugesh previously served as Group CEO of WNS, where he led the company's transformation into a global business services enterprise.
The appointment comes as Chiratae looks to deepen its support for Indian startups as they scale globally, and Murugesh is expected to bring his experience in leadership, organisational transformation, and global expansion to the firm's advisory board.
Zigly Pet Care acquires Prolife Speciality Vet Clinic in Mumbai
Zigly Pet Care has acquired Prolife Speciality Vet Clinic in Malad, Mumbai, marking its third strategic acquisition as the omnichannel pet care brand expands its veterinary healthcare network across India.
Managed by Dr S M Gadge, the clinic has been operational since 2000. Zigly said the acquisition supports its strategy to build a comprehensive pet care ecosystem, with the facility expected to become operational 24x7 over the next nine to 12 months.
Prolife Speciality Vet Clinic has treated close to 20,000 pets and reported an annual recurring revenue of Rs 4.36 crore. The clinic currently offers outpatient consultations, diagnostics, surgery, endoscopy, pathology and pharmacy services. Following the acquisition, it will continue to operate with its existing team of veterinarians, a centre manager and support staff to ensure continuity of care for existing pet parents.
T-Hub launches Flashpoint venture studio to co-build startups with founders
T-Hub has launched Flashpoint, a venture studio that will co-build startups with founders around industry-defined problems. Under the programme, T-Hub and its industry partners will identify specific challenges and select founders to build companies around them.
Selected founders will receive operator-led mentorship and access to infrastructure from day one, including labs, testbeds and existing supply chains. They will also gain access to T-Hub’s network of investors, mentors and resource partners while retaining 100% ownership of their startups with no equity dilution.
Flashpoint is launching with agri-tech and space-tech tracks in partnership with Kheyti and Dhruva Space. Kheyti works on climate-resilient farming solutions for smallholder farmers, while Dhruva Space provides space infrastructure and services, including satellites, mission-critical subsystems, launch facilitation and ground segment solutions. T-Hub is also inviting industry operators and partners to collaborate on additional tracks across sectors.
Eloelo Group launches Dolphin AI
Entertainment and technology company Eloelo Group has unveiled Dolphin AI, an agentic AI studio designed to provide creators with end-to-end video production capabilities. Founder and CEO Saurabh Pandey announced the platform at FICCI FRAMES 2026. Dolphin AI was developed from Eloelo’s own video operations, where its Story TV unit has produced more than 5,000 original dramas and teams test over 100,000 creatives every month. The platform uses multi-shot technology and agentic workflows to address context preservation challenges in AI-generated video, enabling longer and more coherent productions. Dolphin AI can support social media videos, tutorials, D2C advertisements and micro-dramas. Its production environment combines natural-language creation, guided templates, shot-level controls, editing and enhancement within a single workflow for creators, filmmakers, brands and studios.
MrMed reports 123% revenue growth in FY26
Healthtech startup MrMed reported 123% year-on-year revenue growth in FY26, taking revenue to Rs 74.3 crore, while closing the year EBITDA positive. The specialty pharmacy platform served more than one lakh patients during the year, a 63% increase, with orders coming from over 4,000 towns. Nearly 66% of revenue came from outside metro cities, while the company now serves more than 19,000 pincodes. Patients saved Rs 44.3 crore on medicines during FY26, representing an average saving of 41.6%. MrMed covers more than 100 rare diseases across 35 specialty therapy areas and operates cold-chain fulfillment hubs. During FY27, it added hubs in Guwahati and Mumbai. Over the next 12-18 months, the company plans to deepen its presence in Tier II and Tier III markets.
ShepHertz unveils three India-built AI model families
ShepHertz has unveiled three India-built AI model families for machines and missions at Drone Expo 2026. Tatva is designed for on-device command, Sanjaya for fleet and telemetry intelligence, and Drashta for machine vision. The models are part of the company’s AgentAnywhere sovereign AI platform and are designed to operate fully offline on constrained hardware. Tatva converts natural-language instructions into machine commands, while Sanjaya provides fleet intelligence and coordination when connectivity is disrupted. Drashta analyses satellite and aerial imagery within air-gapped environments. ShepHertz said all three models follow a human-in-the-loop approach, with external policies checking model outputs and people approving consequential actions. The company has also opened its trust toolchain under the Apache 2.0 licence, beginning with Shuddhi, a data factory that provides verifiable receipts for AI training datasets.
Roinet Solution launches AI-powered InsurTech platform
Roinet Solution has launched an AI-powered InsurTech platform, targeting ₹500 crore in insurance premiums and one lakh policies by FY28. The company plans to onboard more than 10,000 partners across 22 states, 741-plus districts and over 4,581 cities, with a focus on Tier-2, Tier-3 and rural markets. The platform aims to transform Point of Sales Persons (POSPs) into technology-enabled insurance entrepreneurs by providing customer profiling, real-time product comparisons, recommendations, proposal assistance, policy issuance, renewal tracking, claims support and servicing. Its recommendation engine analyses factors including age, gender, PIN code, pre-existing conditions, tenure and riders. Roinet will also provide POSPs with training, certifications, marketing resources, analytics, income visibility and advisory support. The company plans to work with insurance providers across life, health and motor insurance categories.
Deloitte India and Avolution announce enterprise architecture alliance
Deloitte India and Avolution have announced a strategic alliance to help organisations strengthen enterprise architecture and improve technology and transformation decisions using Avolution’s ABACUS platform. Deloitte India will lead implementation, combining its technology strategy and transformation expertise with ABACUS’ enterprise modelling and impact analysis capabilities. The platform will help organisations develop a connected view of applications, data, technology and AI capabilities, while assessing dependencies, risks and implications of proposed changes. Its AI governance capabilities can also track model usage, risk and compliance across enterprises. The alliance will initially focus on banking, insurance and financial services organisations across South Asia, with India as the lead market. Deloitte and Avolution plan to expand the offering through industry-specific business architecture frameworks and transformation services, with potential opportunities across government, healthcare, telecom, manufacturing and energy.
Freyr Energy appoints Rohit Sharma as brand ambassador
Freyr Energy has appointed India’s World Cup-winning captain Rohit Sharma as its first-ever brand ambassador, launching the nationwide ‘Solar Ho, Toh Freyr Ho!’ campaign. The campaign highlights rooftop solar as a long-term investment and focuses on the importance of dependable installation and servicing. Freyr Energy, which operates across 40-plus cities, has installed more than 20,000 solar systems for homes and businesses. The company said eligible households under the PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana can access government subsidy support of up to Rs 78,000, along with financing options.

articles.title: Microsoft to block Entra ID script injection attacks starting October
articles.text:
Microsoft has reminded customers that the Entra ID identity and access management (IAM) solution will get better protection against external script injection attacks starting next month.
The company first revealed plans to secure Entra ID sign-ins from script injection attacks in a November 2025 announcement.
According to a Monday message center update seen by BleepingComputer, Microsoft will begin enforcing additional Content Security Policy (CSP) defenses that will only allow scripts from trusted Microsoft content delivery network (CDN) domains during Entra ID sign-ins.
The rollout should end by late October 2026, after which all users will be protected from various sign-in security risks, including cross-site scripting attacks in which malicious code is injected into websites to steal credentials.
"Microsoft Entra ID will enhance sign-in security by enforcing a Content Security Policy blocking external script injection starting mid-October 2026," the company said. "This change helps protect users from threats such as cross-site scripting (XSS) by allowing only trusted Microsoft-hosted scripts to run during authentication and blocking unauthorized or externally injected code."
Microsoft advised enterprise customers to stop using browser extensions and tools that inject code or scripts into sign-in pages before the new CSP changes take effect.
It also urged them to test sign-in scenarios before the next month's deadline to identify and address any dependency issues on code-injection tools. IT administrators can identify potential impact by reviewing sign-in flows in the browser developer console and looking for violations that appear in red text with details about the blocked scripts.
"Users will continue to be able to sign in even if unsupported script injection tools no longer function. This change is enabled by default as part of the service update and does not require tenant configuration," the company added.
"Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) and API-based authentication flows are not affected because CSP enforcement applies only to browser-based sign-in experiences using login.microsoftonline.com."
This change is part of Microsoft's Secure Future Initiative (SFI), announced after Chinese hackers breached the Exchange Online mailboxes of dozens of organizations and hundreds of individuals worldwide in May and June 2023.
As part of the same initiative, Microsoft also disabled all ActiveX controls in Windows versions of Microsoft 365 and Office 2024 apps, and it updated Microsoft 365 security defaults to block access to Office, SharePoint, and OneDrive files via legacy authentication protocols.

articles.title: Bientôt la fin des pannes de batterie sur nos voitures : 15 ans de tranquillité assurée avec cette innovation, mais une facture qui double
articles.text:
Bientôt la fin des pannes de batterie sur nos voitures : 15 ans de tranquillité assurée avec cette innovation, mais une facture qui double
Une nouvelle batterie de 12 V pour voiture vient de débuter sa commercialisation aux États-Unis, annonçant une durée de vie allant jusqu’à 15 ans au lieu de 5 ans sur les modèles traditionnels.
La panne de batterie guette chaque conducteur de voiture, immobilisant complètement le véhicule du jour au lendemain. Bonne nouvelle : cette panne pourrait devenir bien moins régulière à l’avenir, avec le lancement d’accumulateurs 12 V solides pouvant tenir pendant une période de 15 ans. Une longévité triplée face au plomb liquide de nos batteries actuelles, qui a comme seul désavantage un prix de vente largement supérieur.
Une batterie solide pour éteindre les craintes de pannes des automobilistes
Pionnière sur le marché des batteries 12 V solides, l’entreprise américaine LiPower commercialise désormais ses solutions auprès du grand public, d’abord aux États-Unis. Si l’addition s’avère salée, entre 400 et 500 $, soit le double des accumulateurs traditionnels, les arguments sont clairement en sa faveur.
En délaissant l’électrolyte liquide des modèles au plomb pour des éléments solides comme les sulfures, les oxydes ou les polymères, ce modèle divise le poids par deux tout en éliminant les risques d’incendie et de fuite corrosive. Il offre aussi une résistance thermique accrue face aux grands froids et ne craint pas les longues périodes d’inactivité.
Résultat : là où une batterie conventionnelle au plomb rend l’âme au bout de quatre à cinq ans, ce modèle solide promet de tenir entre 10 et 15 ans, avec une garantie constructeur de 10 ans. Une longévité record qui permettrait d’éliminer l’angoisse de la panne pour l’ensemble des automobilistes, qu’ils soient en voiture thermique ou en électrique.
Toutefois, la complexité chimique de ces accumulateurs solides vient freiner les cadences de production, retardant ainsi leur déploiement à l’international, et notamment sur le marché européen. D’un autre côté, cette technologie est aussi très attendue sur la batterie principale des voitures électriques, garantissant une autonomie nettement accrue et des temps de recharge bien plus rapides, même en plein hiver.

articles.title: « C’est la folie en ce moment » chez Apple : John Ternus voudrait bouleverser la stratégie du groupe
articles.text:
Le 10 juillet dernier, nous avions jugé la performance de John Ternus lors de sa première keynote. Nous avions trouvé que la passation de pouvoir entre Tim Cook et Ternus était sobre et élégante, mais aussi que le nouveau patron d’Apple avait manqué quelque peu d’audace. Mais cette audace qui semblait manquer lors de l’événement ne pointerait-t-elle pas le bout de son nez, et pas qu’un peu ? Le toujours très bien informé Mark Gurman, journaliste chez Bloomberg, est venu rapporter des discussions de Ternus en interne avec ses collègues, et autant dire qu’un chamboulement semble s’annoncer chez Apple.
Une restructuration chez Apple
Alors que John Ternus occupe le poste de CEO d’Apple depuis maintenant presque un mois, une restructuration s’annonce au sein de l’entreprise. Selon Mark Gurman, Ternus voudrait supprimer certains postes de cadres intermédiaires afin de réduire les niveaux hiérarchiques. Sans grande surprise, Ternus aurait considéré l’intelligence artificielle pour les remplacer, soit une stratégie également étudiée par Mark Zuckerberg. L’objectif serait d’accélérer le développement des produits en supprimant certaines couches hiérarchiques. In fine, Apple présenterait une organisation plus légère, davantage axée sur l’ingénierie.
Plus globalement, Ternus aurait comme objectif de réduire les coûts, tout en trouvant de nouvelles rentrées d’argent. Pour ce faire, l’entreprise miserait sur ses produits existants en proposant de nouveaux services, et donc de nouveaux abonnements. Il faut préciser que le chiffre d’affaires des services d’Apple s’est contracté au deuxième trimestre, une première depuis 2022, même s’il reste supérieur à celui enregistré un an plus tôt. Par ailleurs, l’Apple Store connaît lui aussi un ralentissement de son chiffre d’affaires dans un contexte marqué par de nouvelles réglementations américaines et européennes. John Ternus voudrait ainsi restructurer l’entreprise et se concentrer sur les services, mais pas seulement.
Produire plus, plus fréquemment et dans des délais plus courts
Toujours selon Mark Gurman, John Ternus souhaiterait s’éloigner du calendrier habituel d’Apple, marqué par une keynote au printemps et une autre à l’automne. L’objectif serait de lancer de nouveaux produits à d’autres moments de l’année, et ainsi accélérer le rythme de sortie. Ce nouveau mode opératoire passe inévitablement par une accélération du développement des produits. John Ternus voudrait que les équipes d’Apple livrent plus de produits, plus fréquemment et dans des délais plus courts. Par ailleurs, Ternus souhaiterait que l’entreprise se montre plus expérimentale afin de rester compétitive à l’ère de l’intelligence artificielle.
Une pression conséquente serait d’ores et déjà ressentie par certains employés de l’entreprise. Selon Gurman, l’un d’entre eux, qui a désiré rester anonyme, a expliqué que « tout est beaucoup plus opérationnel qu’avant », avant de préciser ensuite : « C’est la folie en ce moment. » Nous espérions davantage d’audace de la part de John Ternus, mais peut-être pas à ce point.

articles.title: El gran baño de realidad de Yann LeCun: "La idea de tener un país de genios dentro de un centro de datos es una completa tontería"
articles.text:
Hay una frase que se repite en cada lanzamiento de un nuevo modelo de IA: esto es como tener un experto de bolsillo. Sam Altman la usó al presentar GPT-5, comparándolo con "hablar con un experto a nivel de PhD". Alguien lleva meses levantando la mano cada vez que se dice eso.
Yann LeCun, tiene el Premio Turing (el Nobel de la informática) y ayudó a construir buena parte de la IA actual. LeCun ha destacado por su visión pragmática de la evolución de la IA y sostiene abiertamente que esa promesa del "experto en el bolsillo" es puro humo.
El padre de la IA que no se cree el relato. LeCun no encaja en los dos bandos en los que habitualmente se agrupan los líderes de la IA. No pide tirar del freno de emergencia de la IA por miedo a que pueda destruir a la humanidad, pero tampoco comulga con la promesa de la AGI para mañana.
La autoridad que le otorga haber sido uno de los protagonistas de la IA primigenia le permite ver la situación actual de la IA con mayor perspectiva y, como hizo durante una entrevista para Big Technology Podcast, hablar del estado de la IA desde un punto de vista realista: "La idea de que vamos a tener un país de genios dentro de un centro de datos es una completa tontería". Su argumento es muy sencillo de entender: la actual IA es muy buena recordando datos y generando contenido con ellos, pero no son capaces de crear nada desde cero.
"No hay ninguna manera en el infierno". De ese modo, LeCun respondía a afirmación que Dario Amodei hizo en uno de sus ensayos en el que desarrollaba la hipótesis del surgimiento de "un país de genios" en referencia a las capacidades de la IA. " Imaginemos, por ejemplo, 50 millones de personas, todas ellas mucho más capaces que cualquier premio Nobel, estadista o tecnólogo" aseguraba Amodei en su escrito.
La respuesta de LeCun va directa a la línea de flotación de ese argumento: "No vamos a llegar a la IA a nivel humano solo con escalar los LLM. Esto no va a pasar". Y siguió: "Puede parecer que tienes un doctorado al lado, pero no lo es. Es un sistema con memoria y capacidad de recuperación gigantes, no uno que invente soluciones nuevas".
Un LLM no piensa, solo procesa. LeCun cuenta en su entrevista que un LLM típico se entrena con unos 30 billones de tokens. Semejante volumen de información representaría unos 400.000 años de lectura a doce horas diarias para un humano. Es decir, una proporción inabarcable. Y aun así, acumular toda esa información no basta para razonar como una persona.
Un niño de cuatro años ha recibido mediante la vista y el tacto una mayor cantidad de datos en bruto que el modelo más grande jamás entrenado. El mundo físico pesa más que cualquier texto. Según cálculos de Epoch AI, el texto público de calidad en internet ronda los 300 billones de tokens, por lo que los modelso de IA podrían quedarse sin nuevas fuentes de información entre 2026 y 2032. Aunque se quisiera seguir escalando, no habría con qué alimentar a los modelos LLM tal y como los conocemos en la actualidad.
Un punto de realismo para la burbuja de IA. Lo relevante de los argumentos de LeCun no es que dude de la IA, sino dónde se sitúa esa duda. Las tecnológicas vuelcan cientos de miles de millones de dólares en centros de datos bajo la promesa de alcanzar una AGI inminente. Que uno de los padres de la disciplina llame "tontería" a ese relato le da otro matiz. No es un escéptico externo lanzando dardos, es alguien que conoce de primera mano las capacidades de la IA.
No obstante, en la IA no todo es blanco o negro y hay modelos que se han desligado de los LLM convencionales para abrir nuevos caminos en su búsqueda de la AGI. En ese grupo tenemos proyectos como Genie de Google DeepMind, o a Fei-Fei Li con World Labs y su herramienta para la exploración del espacio.

articles.title: Web design : fini les sites rectangulaires, comment CSS Shape va transformer le web
articles.text:
L'aspect des sites internet pourrait bientôt évoluer et se moderniser en abandonnant les éternelles grilles rectangulaires. De nouvelles propriétés de programmation visuelle offrent aux développeurs des solutions pour créer des conceptions fluides sans recourir à des artifices techniques complexes.
Depuis les premières normes de mise en page publiées en 1996, la conception numérique copiait la structure des journaux papier. The Register rappelle que les navigateurs récents intègrent désormais des fonctions qui libèrent les développeurs de ces blocs géométriques stricts.
Des outils de stylisation pour façonner un web non linéaire
Le langage HTML et les feuilles de style CSS imposaient historiquement des bordures strictement horizontales ou verticales sur les pages web. Pour obtenir des présentations originales, les créateurs devaient empiler des modules externes lourds (rappelez-vous… Flash Player, Silverlight…)ou écrire de longues lignes de JavaScript complexes à maintenir. Le format SVG a ensuite permis de tracer des courbes, mais il restait enfermé dans un cadre fixe souvent incapable de s'adapter aux différents écrans. La commande path() a bien tenté de corriger ce problème, mais elle figeait invariablement les dimensions en pixels, rendant les designs peu réactifs (ou "responsives").
Mais récemment, une nouvelle propriété CSS a fait son apparition : shape(). Concrètement, cet outil lit des coordonnées géométriques précises pour dicter une trajectoire directement dans le code du site. Elle utilise une syntaxe native qui comprend de multiples variables et s'adapte automatiquement à l'espace disponible sur la page. Les créateurs l'associent aux propriétés border-shape et corner-shape pour sculpter les bordures physiques de leurs contenus. La première applique le tracé sur les limites du conteneur dès le calcul initial de la page. La seconde fournit un catalogue de motifs prêts à l'emploi, comme des bords joliment biseautés ou le "squircle", un hybride curieux entre le carré et le cercle.
Pour les néophytes, la création manuelle de ces arcs de cercle ou de ces polygones peut paraître complexe. Le développeur Temani Afif explique sur le site CSS-Tricks que ces outils divisent logiquement les formes en catégories : les lignes droites, les courbes, et les motifs répétés. Des convertisseurs gratuits en ligne transforment instantanément vos anciens graphiques SVG en syntaxe shape() parfaitement valide, sans imposer de fastidieux calculs de positionnement spatial. Il devient alors très aisé de dessiner des bulles de discussion, des tickets de cinéma ou de créer un cœur à l'intérieur d'une boîte carrée classique. Les développeurs appliquent aussi des animations fluides pour qu'une forme se modifie ou grandisse au simple passage de la souris.
L'implémentation de ces nouvelles fonctionnalités par l'industrie avance rapidement. La propriété shape() est désormais prise en charge par les principaux navigateurs du marché, comme Chrome 137 ou Safari 18.4. Les éléments border-shape et corner-shape demeurent encore considérés comme expérimentaux par certains acteurs, bien qu'ils fonctionnent déjà très bien sur Edge et Opera.
Au fil du temps les interfaces Web devraient donc devenir plus vivantes sans pour autant compromettre l'accessibilité ou le référencement SEO. Bon heureusement, en cas d'abus (et il y en aura), les extensions activant le mode de lecture minimaliste seront toujours fonctionnelles.

articles.title: Xiaomi 18 Pro : j'ai créé ma propre application pour l'écran arrière, ça m'a pris 5 minutes — Frandroid
articles.text:
Nous avons un Xiaomi 18 Pro chinois à la rédaction afin de découvrir le produit par nous-mêmes avant sa sortie en France. Nous avons d’ailleurs déjà publié nos benchmarks pour éprouver sa nouvelle puce Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 fournie par Qualcomm.
    À lire aussi : 
    Le Xiaomi 18 Pro est-il surpuissant ? On a testé ses performances
Le Xiaomi 18 Pro se distingue surtout par son design atypique doté d’un écran à l’arrière de 2,7 pouces. Grâce à cet écran, vous pouvez vous prendre en selfie avec les capteurs photo arrière tout en ayant un retour caméra. Cela permet de profiter d’une meilleure qualité photo. Notifications et appels entrants peuvent aussi s’y afficher. D’autres fonctions permettent de voir la météo ou son agenda en un coup d’œil, et de contrôler la lecture de la musique en streaming.
Un article dédié est prévu pour tout cela, mais aujourd’hui je voulais me concentrer sur l’une des fonctions phares de cet écran arrière : la génération d’applications par IA.
Vous pouvez, à partir d’un prompt, créer une application dédiée à l’écran arrière. J’ai donc évidemment testé et je voulais vous partager cette première expérimentation.
Mon application : un dé à 20 faces (d20)
Grand amateur de jeux de rôle (et notamment de Donjons et Dragons), j’ai tout de suite pensé à une application simulant le jet d’un d20 (un dé à 20 faces, très utilisé dans ces jeux).
Voici donc ce que ça a donné.
L’interface est en français et dispose de deux boutons :
- Lancer le dé ;
- Remettre à zéro.
Au centre, on voit un icosaèdre (j’ai dû chercher le nom d’une figure géométrique à 20 faces) qui s’anime quand on appuie sur le bouton de lancer de dé avant d’afficher un nombre tiré au hasard entre 1 et 20.
Enfin, à droite, on voit une liste s’afficher comptabilisant la totalité des jets (d’où l’existence d’un bouton de réinitialisation).
Certes, je ne vais pas me précipiter sur cet écran arrière à chacune de mes parties de Donjons et Dragons. Il n’empêche que pour un premier essai, je trouve le résultat concluant, surtout que mon prompt était très basique comme vous allez le voir plus bas dans cet article. Je trouve donc cela assez chouette sur le papier pour les personnes qui seront plus inspirées que moi.
Comment créer une application sur l’écran arrière du Xiaomi 18 Pro
Vous pouvez gérer l’écran arrière du Xiaomi 18 Pro depuis un menu dédié dans les paramètres. La rubrique s’appelle « Affichage arrière ».
Là, il y a une option intitulée « Générez des cartes d’applications grâce à l’IA ». On pense que Xiaomi s’appuie ici sur une version de MiMo, sa famille de modèles d’IA maison.
En appuyant sur ladite rubrique, on tombe sur une interface listant les « applications vedettes », mais c’est le gros bouton + en bas à droite qui nous intéresse.
Ce bouton ouvre un champ de saisie. L’interface HyperOS vous invite à écrire des mots-clés ou à décrire votre idée avec une image. Dans mon cas, j’ai utilisé la saisie vocale du clavier pour énoncer mon idée à l’oral. Voici mon prompt : « Je veux une application simulant un dé à 20 faces, un d20 quoi, sur lequel on peut appuyer pour obtenir un score aléatoire ».
Voici la consigne telle qu’elle a été réécrite par l’IA (l’intégralité du texte dans cette liste à puces a été générée par l’intelligence artificielle).
- Nom : Dé à 20 faces
- Description : Un simple clic sur le dé génère un résultat aléatoire compris entre 1 et 20, l’animation du dé révèle le chiffre obtenu avec un effet de mise en avant, les derniers lancers restent affichés à l’écran et la somme cumulée permet de suivre son score total au fil des parties.
- Style : Géométrique, un dé à vingt faces aux facettes taillées et aux arêtes dorées.
- Couleur : Bleu nuit et violet profond, avec des accents or et blanc cassé.

articles.title: How 297 job applications led Bode Roberts to build Dataleum
articles.text:
When Bode Roberts struggled to break into the workforce, he realised the problem was not his drive; the system itself was broken. So, instead of waiting for a seat at someone else’s table, he built his own. In his latest My Life in Tech feature, JOHN ADOYI chronicles how Roberts turned years of job-hunting silence into Dataleum, an award-winning EdTech platform transforming African talent into a global export.
297 applications. 48 interviews. Three years without a job.
For Bode Roberts, co-founder of the edtech platform Dataleum, those numbers were more than a record of an unsuccessful job search. They represented three years of hope, rejection, and uncertainty, and eventually forced him to confront what it meant to measure his worth by whether someone would employ him.
“It was a cycle of hope followed by the heavy silence of rejection,” Roberts says.
Some interviews seemed promising. Some applications carried the possibility that things might finally change. Then came the silence, again and again.
“There were moments of genuine confusion and tears,” he says. “The weight of ‘not having work’ began to feel like a commentary on my worth.”
The experience changed the question Roberts was asking. Instead of asking how he could find his place in the workforce, he began thinking about how to make it easier for others to find theirs.
Looking back, Roberts says the experience changed how he understood unemployment.
“I realised that if someone with my background and drive was struggling this much, the system itself was broken,” he says.
That realisation changed the question he was trying to answer. Instead of asking how he could find his place in the workforce, Roberts began thinking about how to make it easier for others to find theirs.
Years later, that shift would help shape Dataleum, the edtech platform he co-founded.
“I am actually grateful for those 48 rejections,” Roberts says. “They were the fuel I needed to build my own table.”
But Roberts’ concern with opportunity began long before he started applying for jobs.
His understanding of opportunity began taking shape in childhood.
Roberts attended a private school while his mother taught in the public school system. He says he sometimes accompanied her to work, where he saw classrooms meant for dozens of pupils packed with more than 300 children. He also saw students sitting on the floor and struggling with basic literacy.
“Talent is universal, but opportunity is not,” Roberts says.
Roberts says he also spent much of his childhood around people older than him. While other children played typical playground games, he played Monopoly, Ludo and cards with adult neighbours.
“Those weren’t just games; they were my first lessons in negotiation, strategic thinking, and emotional intelligence,” he says. “My environment taught me how to navigate spaces where I was the youngest person in the room.”
He says he was drawn to numbers from an early age and became the top mathematics student in his primary school. In 2002, he won the Milo Nestlé award for his mathematical abilities. His interest in solving problems also led him to start his first business while he was still in secondary school.
In 2009, Roberts began studying Computer Engineering at Covenant University, a private university in Ogun State, southwest Nigeria. But he was interested in more than how machines worked. He wanted to understand how technology could be used to solve problems for people.
He treated his university years as a period of experimentation. Roberts says he started about 16 businesses as an undergraduate, using each one to learn about suppliers, customers, marketing, negotiation, and sales.
“Those weren’t just side hustles; they were my real-world classroom,” he says. “I was negotiating with suppliers, sourcing products, managing customer experiences, and marketing to my peers.”
He graduated in 2014 and later pursued a master’s degree in Production and Operations Management because, he says, he wanted to understand how technology could be implemented and scaled within businesses.
His time at Lagos Business School further changed how he thought about building businesses. Roberts says the programme shifted his focus from business survival to long-term sustainability.
“It wasn’t just about learning theory; it was about building relationships with leaders across various sectors who were all grappling with the same question: How do we build businesses that last in Africa?” he says.
After school, Roberts moved into banking. It was there, while working at a financial institution, that he said he encountered a problem that would later lead to Dataleum.
Despite working in a high-growth environment, he says he struggled to find accessible opportunities to upskill. Training was either unavailable or too expensive.
He discussed the problem with his friend and future co-founder, Titilola Bello. They realised that if working professionals were struggling to access quality digital training, the problem could be even greater for unemployed young people.
That conversation became the starting point for Dataleum.
Building Dataleum
Roberts and Bello tested the idea before building a business around it. Roberts says they spoke to 20 people during an early feasibility study, 15 of whom validated the need for accessible and affordable digital skills training.
When they launched their first marketing campaign, 27 people expressed interest. One organisation then paid upfront for 10 training slots, giving Dataleum its first revenue.
“That initial revenue allowed us to build gradually,” Roberts says.
As the company grew, it began working with organisations including the Lagos State Employment Trust Fund, Access Bank, the United Nations, Coca-Cola and Flutterwave.
Building Dataleum also meant making a difficult decision about his career. Roberts left his banking job to lead the company full-time, a move he says was followed by “incredibly rough” months that tested his resolve.
Seven months after Dataleum launched, the company was still operating from a physical training centre when the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted operations in March 2020. It forced Dataleum to rethink how it delivered training.
In March 2020, Dataleum launched a virtual data hackathon, or what he calls “Datathon”. The event brought data analysts from different locations together online.
“Despite the global standstill, we saw data analysts from all over logging in to compete,” he says.
Roberts says the Datathon changed how he viewed Dataleum’s reach. What had started as a physical training centre in Lagos could now bring people together regardless of where they were.
Dataleum expanded into the UK in 2023. Roberts says it became a registered learning centre with the UK Register of Learning Providers within two months.
But the expansion exposed a different challenge. Roberts says many Nigerian Dataleum alumni who had moved to the UK were struggling to navigate the labour market, particularly those from underrepresented groups and people of colour.
“While Nigeria is a familiar, high-volume market for us, the UK is a market of high standards and specific community needs,” he says.
Roberts says Dataleum responded by placing greater emphasis on community-building and support for immigrants and minority communities navigating the UK labour market.
Three years after Dataleum launched, the company won the Lagos State Startup of the Year award. In 2023, it also received the Best EdTech Startup in Africa award at the Global Startup Awards.
“Standing on a stage with innovators from across the globe and hearing Dataleum named the best on the continent was a profound testament to our impact,” he says.
Becoming a builder
Running Dataleum has also changed how Roberts thinks about leadership.
He says he began as an operator, shaped by the hands-on approach he developed while running businesses at university. When Dataleum launched, he was still experimenting with different leadership styles as he worked to get the company off the ground.
As the company grew and he began leading professionals from different generations, Roberts says he realised that leadership required something different.
“High-performance teams aren’t built on ‘command and control,’ but on servant leadership,” he says. “To lead the younger generation, you must be a listener.”
Today, Roberts describes himself as moving into what he calls the “Legacy Builder” phase. His focus, he says, is less on managing every operation and more on creating an environment where other leaders can emerge.
“My goal is no longer just to manage operations, but to architect an environment where other leaders can emerge. I want to ensure that impact isn’t just something we do internally; I want to inspire a movement of young leaders who are on that same ‘impact thread.’”
That shift is tied to what Roberts sees as a larger challenge for Africa. He calls the continent’s talent the “African Asset” and believes much of it remains untapped.
“I believe African talent is the untapped engine the world needs to solve its most complex problems,” he says. “My greatest pressure is ensuring we are building the right infrastructure to make that talent economically viable.”
For Roberts, the impact of developing talent extends beyond the person who takes a course or gets a job. He says he also thinks about the families and businesses that can benefit when people gain access to better opportunities.
“It’s not just about the student who takes a course today,” he says. “It’s about the family that is lifted out of poverty because that student got a global job.”
His experience with the UNDP’s Young Africa Innovates programme in 2025 also exposed him to entrepreneurs who are often excluded from mainstream opportunities, including people with disabilities and founders from underserved communities. Roberts says the experience reinforced his belief that Africa’s progress must include people who are often left behind.
For Roberts, the longer-term goal is to build systems and develop people who can outlast his time as CEO.
“I want to ensure that impact isn’t just something we do internally,” he says. “My leadership today is about building systems and people that will outlast my own tenure as CEO.”
‘The catalyst of human potential’
Roberts’ ambitions now extend beyond Dataleum. Over the next 10 years, he wants the company to become what he describes as a sustainable African talent ecosystem, helping Africa move from consuming technology to exporting innovation.
He is also pursuing a PhD at Covenant University on the impact of artificial intelligence on operational efficiency in systemically important banks. Roberts says he wants to understand how emerging technologies can be applied in the African context and contribute to global knowledge.
But when asked what would remain if everything he had built disappeared, Roberts returns to the qualities that existed before Dataleum, the awards and the titles.
“At my core, I am a practitioner of ‘opportunity maximization.’ Even with nothing, I would still have my faith in God, the resilience my parents instilled in me, and the integrity that has guided every decision.”
He says he would still be a builder, with problems to solve and people to empower.
“I hope the narrative isn’t about the awards I won, but about the thousands of tables I helped create for others to sit at,” he says.

articles.title: WatchGuard Patches Critical Fireware OS Code Injection Vulnerability
articles.text:
WatchGuard on Tuesday announced fixes for 15 vulnerabilities in Fireware OS, including a critical-severity remote code execution (RCE) bug.
Tracked as CVE-2026-86131 (CVSS score of 9.2), the flaw is described as a code injection issue in how the operating system handles BOVPN over TLS client configurations.
Successful exploitation could allow a remote attacker who controls the remote VPN server to execute commands with root privileges on the connecting Firebox appliance.
The security weakness was resolved in Fireware OS versions 2026.3.2, 2026.2.3, 12.12.3, and 12.5.21.
The security updates also resolve 13 high-severity vulnerabilities that could lead to RCE, authorization bypass, denial-of-service (DoS), unauthorized SSLVPN access, and arbitrary local file reads.
A medium-severity improper authorization issue leading to unauthorized access to web applications was also addressed.
Several of these security defects could be exploited by remote attackers without authentication.
The Fireware OS patches landed one day after WatchGuard rolled out fixes for two critical- and one high-severity Access Point flaws.
Tracked as CVE-2026-101891 and CVE-2026-86102 and affecting internal API services, the critical issues could be exploited to obtain a valid API session without authentication and execute arbitrary shell commands on the underlying OS.
The high-severity weakness is an OS command injection that requires administrative privileges for exploitation. All three vulnerabilities were resolved in WatchGuard AP version 3.4.8.
According to WatchGuard, it is not aware of any of these security issues being exploited in the wild. Additional information can be found on the company’s security advisories page.

articles.title: OpenAI planea recibir USD 30.000 millones de inversores: la empresa costaría 1,4 billones de dólares
articles.text:
OpenAI negocia con inversores una nueva ronda de financiamiento de al menos USD 30.000 millones que llevaría su valuación a unos 1,4 billones de dólares, informó Bloomberg.
Según la agencia, las negociaciones se encuentran en una etapa temprana y podrían cambiar. De concretarse, la ronda funcionaría como un puente de capital privado en lugar de la salida a bolsa que la empresa había contemplado para este año, pero que finalmente no se concretó y por ahora no tiene fecha establecida.
PUBLICIDAD
La cifra representaría un salto respecto de la última ronda conocida de la compañía: en marzo, OpenAI recaudó 122.000 millones de dólares en una operación que la valuó en 852.000 millones, con Amazon, Nvidia y SoftBank como principales inversores y Microsoft también participando.
Cómo sería el salto en los ingresos de OpenAI
El ingreso anualizado de OpenAI superó los 40.000 millones de dólares en agosto, un salto del 70% desde julio, según había reportado Bloomberg semanas atrás. La cifra es una proyección basada en el ritmo de ventas de un período determinado, no una medición directa de ingresos anuales ya facturados.
De cerrarse en los términos actuales, la nueva valuación volvería a ubicar a OpenAI por encima de Anthropic, su principal competidora, que había superado momentáneamente a la compañía de Sam Altman a comienzos de año en el mercado privado.
PUBLICIDAD
La ronda llega después de que Altman descartara una salida a bolsa durante 2026 para priorizar la seguridad de sus modelos. “Creo que es inaceptable estar tomando algo así como un 10% de posibilidades de matar a todos para fines de la década”, dijo el ejecutivo a la revista Fortune, en referencia a las advertencias de otros actores del sector sobre los riesgos de la inteligencia artificial avanzada.
OpenAI frena el desarrollo de su IA
Esta semana, OpenAI anunció que no lanzará GPT-6.1 Astra, la versión más avanzada de su modelo insignia, después de determinar que el sistema mostraba una disposición alta a engañar a los usuarios sobre sus propias acciones. En su lugar, la empresa presentó una versión más económica llamada Sol.
PUBLICIDAD
Altman también respaldó una propuesta del director ejecutivo de Anthropic, Dario Amodei, para frenar el desarrollo de los modelos más avanzados de IA e incorporar evaluadores externos que auditen su seguridad.
La directora financiera de OpenAI, Sarah Friar, había advertido puertas adentro que un crecimiento de ingresos más lento podría dejar a la empresa sin capacidad para cumplir sus contratos futuros de cómputo, según informó The Wall Street Journal. Friar también planteó dudas sobre si la compañía estaba en condiciones de cumplir con los requisitos regulatorios del mercado bursátil en los plazos que prefería Altman.
La presión regulatoria se suma a una serie de incidentes con agentes de IA de la empresa, entre ellos episodios vinculados a la plataforma Hugging Face y a un sitio web del gobierno de Australia, que OpenAI todavía investiga.
PUBLICIDAD
Qué viene ahora para la empresa de ChatGPT
El anuncio de la ronda coincidió con la jornada de DevDay, la conferencia anual para desarrolladores de OpenAI, donde la empresa presentó Dots, un asistente que ejecuta tareas de forma autónoma a través de aplicaciones como Slack y Teams con supervisión limitada.
Según Bloomberg, la compañía también recortó algunos límites de uso disponibles para los suscriptores de su plan de 200 dólares mensuales, en medio del esfuerzo por sostener el ritmo de gastos que exige la expansión de su infraestructura.
Las fuentes consultadas por la agencia insistieron en que ningún monto ni la estructura final de la ronda están cerrados, y que el resultado dependerá de cómo avancen las conversaciones con los inversores en las próximas semanas.

articles.title: Trump plan to combat AI risks hinges on Big Tech pals policing themselves
articles.text:
Amid escalating AI security incidents causing OpenAI to halt training and pause releases, Donald Trump continues to advocate for the AI industry to regulate itself as the best path to combat emerging risks when developing frontier AI.
In an agreement Tuesday, two dozen tech firms voluntarily committed to implementing controls recommended by the White House, including undergoing independent safety audits that will test whether firms’ internal controls, monitoring, and detecting are actually working. Key focuses for external reviews included “risks related to cybersecurity, biosecurity, chemical threats, and unintended actions by AI models.”
Firms also agreed to regularly meet to discuss best practices and set common AI safety standards and benchmarks. Among signers were leaders like Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Alphabet/Google’s Sundar Pichai.
Nothing new is legally required of firms, and some—like Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI—had already committed to external audits, The Information reported. Additionally, many firms have voluntarily committed to highly secretive government safety testing. Adding to these tests, Trump insisted the Tuesday deal will somehow better address real emerging risks and is “morally binding,” despite carrying no legal weight, Bloomberg reported.
“It’s almost like a constitution, in a way,” Trump told reporters at the White House following a lunch with tech leaders. “The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection.”
Eventually, it “may make sense to codify” the recommendations, the agreement said near the end. But for now, Trump stressed that the best possible future for the US requires trusting AI firms to regulate themselves.
Trump’s Big Tech friends embrace “SI”
So far, very few details have been released about how the new round of safety audits would work. Trump has only posted a summary of the accord on Truth Social.
It’s also unclear who Trump is tapping to audit frontier models. Bloomberg noted that Trump seems to be politicizing the selection process, while some AI firms appear uncertain what might qualify as a third party to test their frontier AI. Some progress has been made already in finding candidates, though, as Bloomberg reported that “some of the firms poised to conduct those reviews have already met” with the US agency conducting voluntary government pre-deployment safety tests, the Center for AI Standards and Innovation.

articles.title: Cryptography was the last slow problem | EU-Startups
articles.text:
On 28 July of this year, it took an AI about sixty hours to find a cryptographic flaw that two years of expert review had not uncovered.
In the following 24 hours, the findings were confirmed and the digital signature submission intended to be secure against both classical and quantum computers, HAWK – a lattice‑based post‑quantum signature scheme under evaluation – was withdrawn from consideration. It will never be standardised.
A static security system
For fifty years, cryptography has been the one part of technology you could pretty much set and forget. RSA, a foundational public-key cryptography algorithm used for secure data transmission, arrived in 1977, became mainstream in web traffic security by 1994, and is still useful today.
Minor attacks on it have accumulated slowly, parameters have increased, and it has taken decades for meaningful advances.
That slowness has been baked into everything we have built with cryptography: standards bodies deliberate for years, migration programmes are planned in five-year blocks, and procurement assumes that what you buy today will still be adequate in 2033.
Even the US government’s Executive Order 14412 that moved post-quantum deadlines to 2030 and 2031 is considered aggressive. They pulled the timeline forward by half a decade and the industry called it a shock. However –
Sixty hours.
AI broke one candidate algorithm in no time at all, changing the price of the discovery cycle. When the time required to find a cryptographic weakness collapses from years to days, and the time required to fix a weakness across a large organisation stays at years, you are left with a gap. Bad things live in that gap.
The uncomfortable arithmetic is that the half-life of a cryptographic assumption may now be plausibly shorter than the duration of a cryptographic migration project. If that is even a possible truth, then every organisation whose plan is “arrive at post-quantum by 2030” has been designed for the wrong world.
The nearing threat
The realistic AI threat to encryption over the next three years actually has almost nothing to do with breaking an algorithm, but in implementation.
Every large organisation is carrying cryptography throughout: expired certificates later renewed with a weak key, a service still negotiating a deprecated cipher suite, a hardcoded credential in a repository that arrived with an acquisition in 2019, a random number generator that perhaps isn’t very random.
A new economics in finding the flaw has developed. Discovering a flaw took highly skilled humans to go looking, and the obscure corners of the enterprise were protected only due to the fact auditing them wasn’t worth anyone’s time.
AI has just changed that. Attackers can easily and continuously read all code, certificates and network configurations at next to zero cost. Every weakness should now be assumed to be found.
Nothing I have described requires a quantum computer to exist, only what already happened in July: finding cryptographic weakness became dramatically cheaper, and fixing it has become no faster.
Even if Q-Day, the hypothetical moment when quantum computers become powerful enough to break standard public-key encryption, never comes, every word of this still holds because you will be exposed to AI-assisted attackers exploiting classical flaws.
Cryptographic agility is the unusual security investment that pays out under every scenario.
A surprisingly humdrum solution
His four core banking platforms: two of them inherited through acquisitions; several thousand certificates across three cloud providers; payments integration whose cryptography is contractually the supplier’s responsibility.
This is a capable person, well-funded, running an expert team at a serious institution describing the reality of the industry.
You cannot fix what you cannot find, which is why a cryptographic inventory matters, and why the June executive order directs CISA, working with NIST, to publish guidance on the minimum elements of a “cryptographic bill of materials” by March 2027.
Inventory tells you where you stand. Agility is the ability to move. In practice, that means four things: knowing what cryptography you run and where it lives; being able to replace an algorithm without rewriting the application; requiring your suppliers to demonstrate they can do the same; and having actually exercised all of it, at least once.
That last one is what everybody skips. A migration capability you have never used is a disaster recovery plan you have never tested.
What next?
I would encourage all companies not to wait until March 2027 for CISA to define what a cryptographic bill of materials ought to contain. This quarter, ask your security to lead the question I asked that CISO in the spring. If the answer is longer than a week, you have found your project.
Q-Day may well be a decade away. What’s for certain is that the sixty hours have already happened, and that nothing about most organisations’ ability to respond changed that week, and losing that gap is entirely within your control.

articles.title: OpenAI takes on Meta Muse with always-on Dots agents, less than a day after delaying GPT-6.1 Astra over safety concerns
articles.text:
What just happened? With Meta's Muse AI agent getting a lot of attention right now, OpenAI has launched its own always-on personal agent that it says can do nearly anything. The release comes a day after the company announced it was delaying the release of GPT-6.1 Astra due to safety concerns discovered during testing.
Called Dots, the agents were unveiled at OpenAI's DevDay conference on Tuesday. They run on the existing GPT-6 Astra model, with each getting its own cloud computer and browser. OpenAI says its plugin ecosystem lets them connect to more than 4,000 apps and keep working toward users' goals around the clock.
The idea is an assistant that learns your preferences and takes care of ongoing jobs without needing instructions for every step. OpenAI says one early tester's dot spotted an invoice he had forgotten to send, prepared it, and sent it after getting his approval.
Users can contact their dot through ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams, with texting coming later. They can also inspect its computer or give it access to their own laptop.
It goes without saying that handing an AI access to your accounts requires a fair amount of trust, which a lot of people aren't going to have. OpenAI says Dots' unsolicited background research uses read-only tools, so those research tasks cannot send messages, alter connected apps, or control a browser. Follow-up actions face separate checks, while purchases require approval and password changes remain the user's responsibility.
It might not be an ideal time to release an AI product with that much potential control. Less than 24 hours before Dots was announced, OpenAI held back GPT-6.1 Astra after researchers raised concerns about its behavior. Safety chief Saachi Jain said the model had become more persistent at completing tasks, but the company needed to balance that against unauthorized actions.
Muse has already shown some of the complications involved. Meta rolled back an internal experiment using human contractors to handle calls after employees raised privacy concerns. One contractor also made a racist remark during a call. There was also an incident in which Muse gave out a user's home address without permission to a person on Facebook Marketplace and invited them to the location.
There are other issues beyond privacy. Amazon has blocked Muse's shopping attempts, arguing that the agent failed to identify itself properly. The retailer is also working to block rival agents from Google and OpenAI, which could put a dent in those do-anything promises.
Dots are rolling out to Pro and Business Premium subscribers in eligible markets, with the first agent included at no extra charge. Enterprise, Edu, and Healthcare customers can try the beta if their administrator enables it.

articles.title: Where to draw the line on AI: Lessons from digital forensics
articles.text:
Where to draw the line on AI: Lessons from digital forensics
Where AI helps, and where it shouldn’t
Artificial intelligence is becoming part of almost every workflow. Developers are using it to write and test code, customer support is turning to it to handle routine queries, and security teams are using it to analyze alerts and support investigations. Digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) is no exception.
DFIR Curriculum Lead and Head of Faculty at SANS Institute.
But as digital forensics work has evolved over the last few decades, one lesson remains consistent. Tools can support investigations, but investigators remain responsible for the quality of the conclusions they reach. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into workflows across industries, the challenge is understanding where AI tools can assist and where human expertise remains essential – and importantly, where organizations should draw the line.
Where AI adds value
For digital forensics and incident response teams, some of AI's most promising applications are also its most practical.
With 90 percent of criminal investigations and prosecutions now involving a digital element, DFIR teams are being asked to process enormous volumes of data. As of February of this year, more than 20,000 devices remain in the digital forensics backlog in England and Wales alone.
Data is spread across endpoints, cloud environments, communications platforms and user accounts, and AI can help investigators triage. It can process that information more efficiently and help to identify potential leads, spot connections between datasets, and highlight other sources of evidence that may require further examination.
For example, it can help investigators correlate relevant activity across multiple devices, accounts and data sources, supporting the reconstruction of events timelines that would otherwise take days to piece together manually. It can also help practitioners organize information and structure reports, allowing them to spend less time on administrative work and more time on analysis.
Used appropriately, AI can reduce the time spent on manual, repetitive work and allow skilled practitioners to spend more time on the analysis and decision-making that moves their work forward.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The danger of treating AI as an answer
The challenge is that AI often appears so authoritative that people become overly reliant on its outputs.
One of the most important lessons from digital forensics is that every tool has limitations. Experienced investigators understand that forensic tools can be wrong. AI is no different. The greatest risk of AI is using it without having the foundational knowledge needed to recognize when it is wrong.
AI is like your junior analyst on their best day. It can identify patterns, highlight areas of interest and help move work forward. But no organization would allow a junior analyst to make the final decision in a sensitive investigation without oversight and accountability. AI should be approached in much the same way.
Problems arise when organizations treat AI-generated outputs as answers rather than something that needs to be validated by someone with the expertise to challenge them. AI can help you reach a conclusion, but it shouldn’t be the conclusion in and of itself.
Knowing where to draw the line
There are many areas where AI can accelerate and enhance work, but there are some areas where AI should never be used. Organizations need to pay attention to where those boundaries lie.
In digital forensics, AI can help identify information that warrants further examination. It can support analysis and help investigators work more efficiently. But it shouldn’t be blindly trusted to reach investigative conclusions or determine innocence or guilt.
Those decisions carry legal, professional and life-changing consequences, making human judgement and accountability non-negotiable.
The same principle extends beyond digital forensics. Organizations in every sector are now deciding how much responsibility should be handed to AI. The answer will vary depending on the use case, but the underlying question remains the same - what safeguards are in place to prevent people becoming overly reliant on AI outputs, and how will they know when those outputs are wrong?
Building frameworks for responsible adoption
These are exactly the questions currently being addressed by the new practical frameworks for the use of AI in digital forensics and incident response. They encourage organizations to consider how much risk a task carries, how outputs will be reviewed, and where human oversight should remain mandatory.
Using AI in DFIR requires strict governance because the stakes are so high. Mistakes are taken seriously when someone’s life is on the line, or a wrongful conviction could take place. However, it shouldn’t take consequences this severe for organizations to work towards protecting the integrity of their decision-making and ensuring humans remain in the driving seat.
Rather than racing to embed AI into every process, organizations should establish governance frameworks first – including what AI should never be in charge of – then start with low-risk use cases where outputs can be easily reviewed or reversed. From there, they can expand capability and explore how AI can help their teams do their jobs better, acting as a force-multiplier rather than the final arbiter.

articles.title: Nuvacore reveals unconventional Core First CPU IP design strategy — chip startup led by Apple and Nuvia legends plans to delay ISA selection for as long as possible
articles.text:
Nuvacore reveals unconventional Core First CPU IP design strategy — chip startup led by Apple and Nuvia legends plans to delay ISA selection for as long as possible
The return of AMD's ambidextrous strategy?
When Nuvacore, a new CPU startup founded by legendary CPU and system architects Gerard Williams, John Bruno, and Ram Srinivasan, emerged from stealth earlier this year, it promised to "rewrite the rules of silicon," but did not say how it planned to do so. On Thursday, the company finally broke its silence and revealed that it is taking an unusual development approach that allows it to design a significant portion of its CPU core IP before committing to a particular instruction set architecture (ISA).
Traditionally, CPU developers start development of a new processor project with a particular ISA — such as Arm, RISC-V, or x86 — already selected. Although modern high-performance processors translate instructions into internal micro-operations and therefore separate the ISA from much of the underlying execution pipelines, the instruction set still influences numerous architectural decisions, including instruction decoding, register handling, memory ordering, and, of course, software compatibility.
Nuvacore says its Core First approach reverses at least part of this process. Instead of designing WarpCore around the requirements and limitations of a predetermined ISA, the company's engineers are developing a significant portion of the foundational CPU IP independent of a particular ISA. To a large degree, one can compare such an approach to the development of a car around its engine and not trying to fit an engine into an already developed platform.
"Rather than beginning with the constraints of an existing architecture and iterating from there, we are starting with the core itself," the company said in its statement.
As a result, the team may be able to better focus on the core's microarchitecture and optimize it for performance, power efficiency, and sustained workloads typical of modern data centers and AI infrastructure, the target application for the company. Nuvacore intends to select an instruction set later based on what works best for the systems that it and its partners plan to build.
There are obvious limits to how ISA-independent a CPU design can be. Eventually, WarpCore will need front-end logic designed around its chosen instruction set, and those architectural requirements will inevitably affect other parts of the processor. Nevertheless, substantial pieces of a modern CPU — such as execution units, branch-prediction units, data paths, caches, and portions of the memory subsystem — can be developed and evaluated before every ISA-related implementation decision is finalized.
In addition to not disclosing its ISA, which is arguably the biggest unanswered question surrounding the project, Nuvacore also has not disclosed the project's schedule, configuration, manufacturing process, power, or performance targets, though given the lack of the ISA commitment, one could say that the remaining details are not that important.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
For now, the only thing that Nuvacore discloses about WarpCore is that it is "a new class of general-purpose CPU designed specifically for the sustained performance and power-efficiency requirements of AI infrastructure and contemporary data centers."
AMD's ambidextrous strategy returns?
Nuvacore's approach is not entirely without precedent. Under CEOs Rory Read and Lisa Su, AMD spent part of the 2010s pursuing an "ambidextrous" strategy intended to let it address x86 and Arm customers by sharing substantial processor and platform IP.
Arguably the most detailed part of the initiative was AMD's SkyBridge platform, announced in 2014. Under SkyBridge, AMD envisioned pin-compatible 64-bit Arm and x86 systems-on-chips that were to use AMD's own Puma+ x86 cores and Arm's Cortex-A57 cores with common platform infrastructure. Separately, AMD developed its custom 64-bit Arm K12 core under Jim Keller that was supposed to share microarchitecture features with Zen. Ultimately, due to lack of resources, SkyBridge was ultimately scrapped, while K12 never became a commercial product as AMD only pursued x86 Zen cores. The difference is, of course, that Nuvacore appears to be taking the idea further by deliberately postponing the ISA decision for WarpCore.
Since Nuvacore is still just a startup, we can only wonder whether its business plan includes marketing of CPUs at all. Nuvia, which was also founded by Williams and Bruno along with Manu Gulati, was acquired by Qualcomm and ultimately shaped the company's Snapdragon X Elite SoCs. In that light, its approach could give the company considerable commercial flexibility.
By developing much of its WarpCore design without tying it to a particular ISA, the company could potentially adapt the technology to the requirements of a future customer or partner. An Arm licensee could use the underlying core technology for an Arm implementation; another customer could choose RISC-V or another ISA. An established x86 vendor could potentially acquire or license the underlying microarchitecture and create its own x86 CPUs if it needs to.
Nuvacore, of course, has not indicated that such a transaction is its objective, but keeping WarpCore ISA-agnostic for as long as possible potentially broadens the number of companies to which its CPU technology could be valuable.
All in all, the Core First announcement tells us considerably more about how Nuvacore intends to develop WarpCore than what the processor itself will eventually look like. But if the company really does keep its ISA options open until relatively late in development, WarpCore represents an unusual attempt to separate development of a high-performance CPU microarchitecture from one of the decisions that normally defines a processor project from its earliest stages.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.
