articles.title: Voyeurisme sordide ou science ? La nouvelle série de Netflix choque les spectateurs
articles.text:
En 1971, l’expérience de Stanford, menée avec 24 étudiants tous masculins, devait durer deux semaines. Elle s’était arrêtée au bout de six jours dans un bain de larmes, de maltraitances psychologiques et de sadisme incontrôlé. Un désastre éthique devenu le cas d’école de tout ce qu’il ne faut pas faire en sciences humaines. Plus d’un demi-siècle plus tard, Netflix en a fait une série de six épisodes de 45 minutes.
Prévue pour le 21 octobre 2026, la série Netflix de téléréalité enferme pendant deux semaines 30 volontaires (hommes et femmes, cette fois) dans un vrai pénitencier, filmées 24 heures sur 24 par des caméras télécommandées. La productrice exécutive Jane Lipsitz a beau jurer sur tous les toits que son équipe a prévu des « garde-fous », des psychologues 24/7 et des mots de passe pour abandonner, la ficelle est trop grosse. Présenter ce divertissement comme une « réinvention moderne » de la célèbre étude revient à emballer de la téléréalité trash dans du papier cadeau universitaire.
Une série Netflix qui pose question
Il n’a pas fallu plus de quelques heures après l’annonce de la série, pour que les réseaux sociaux s’enflamment. Sur X, l’incompréhension a très vite laissé place au dégoût et à l’ironie mordante.
Avec une éthique vendue au clic, les internautes s’insurgent contre le cynisme de la plateforme. « Est-ce qu’on fait vraiment ça ou est-ce qu’on fait juste semblant que les comités d’éthique n’existent plus pour le bien de l’algorithme ? », s’interroge une utilisatrice, tandis qu’un autre résume le projet d’une formule assassine : « L’original a été stoppé après six jours et Netflix a répondu : ‘Hold my beer, on va en faire un truc à binger’. »
Plusieurs internautes rappellent que la méthode de 1971 a depuis été démontée. Dans son enquête Histoire d’un mensonge (2018), le chercheur français Thibault Le Texier a montré, archives à l’appui, que les gardiens avaient reçu des consignes de Zimbardo avant l’expérience. « Le pire, c’est que l’expérience d’origine était bidonnée. Les gardes étaient poussés à être violents », rappelle un internaute.
D’autres ironisent sur la différence fondamentale entre une étude de 1971 et une émission de 2026 : « Zimbardo a tout coupé au bout de six jours. Une émission de télé a toutes les raisons du monde de laisser tourner les caméras. »
La critique ne vient pas seulement des internautes. Clay Ramsay, le « prisonnier 416 » de l’expérience originale, qui avait fait une grève de la faim en 1971, a confié à Newsweek qu’il craignait que la série brouille la frontière entre divertissement et science.
Du laboratoire au divertissement de masse
Pour désamorcer la polémique, la production met en avant un casting mixte, des tests psychologiques avant l’entrée en prison et trois experts : Alison Wood Brooks, psychologue comportementale à Harvard, Trymaine Lee, journaliste lauréat du prix Pulitzer, et Michael Cantrell, ancien professionnel de l’administration pénitentiaire fédérale, avec près de trente ans de carrière.
La vraie perversion du projet réside dans le dispositif lui-même. La simulation s’installe dans une vraie prison, au milieu d’authentiques détenus qui servent de décor d’ambiance. En prétendant répondre à la question « le pouvoir corrompt-il ? », Netflix réutilise en réalité la mécanique la plus ancienne du genre : enfermer des cobayes dans un bocal social pour observer jusqu’où la pression les fera craquer. À la différence près qu’ici, on habille le spectacle du vernis respectable de la science comportementale.
La télévision a déjà tenté l’exercice. En 2002, la BBC a diffusé The Experiment, où les psychologues Alex Haslam et Steve Reicher reproduisaient l’étude de Stanford. Un comité d’éthique suivait le tournage sur place, et les chercheurs se contentaient d’observer, alors que Zimbardo dirigeait lui-même sa prison. Les prisonniers ont fini par se serrer les coudes pour obtenir de meilleures conditions, à l’opposé du scénario de 1971.
Il faudra attendre la mise en ligne des six épisodes, le 21 octobre, pour savoir ce que les participants ont vécu pendant ces deux semaines.

articles.title: Wie Autofahrer ihre Fahrzeuge selbst um autonome Fahrfunktionen erweitern – und warum das ein Problem ist
articles.text:
Wie Autofahrer ihre Fahrzeuge selbst um autonome Fahrfunktionen erweitern – und warum das ein Problem ist
Wer autonomes Fahren nutzen will, musste tief in die Tasche greifen. Denn nur die aktuellen Fahrzeuge von Tesla und Co. unterstützen FSD und das auch nur in einigen Regionen der Welt. Ein Unternehmen aus den USA verspricht jetzt, zumindest die finanziellen Hürden zu eliminieren. Sie bieten ein vergleichsweise günstiges Nachrüstkit für autonomes Fahren an, das auch ältere Fahrzeuge unterstützt.
Comma AI: Autonomes Fahren für alle?
Insgesamt kann das „Comma Four“ in mehr als 350 Fahrzeugen verbaut werden, sofern sie schon Kameras vorinstalliert haben. Im Grunde handelt es sich dabei um ein kleines Gerät, an die Windschutzscheibe geklebt wird, um mit integrierten Kameras nach vorn „sehen“ zu können. Zusätzlich wird das Gadget über Kabel mit den von Werk aus eingebauten Kameras des Fahrzeuges verbunden.
Auf der Softwareseite kommt „Openpilot“ zum Einsatz. Das Open-Source-Modell kann automatisch die Spur halten, beschleunigen und bremsen und dadurch laut Comma AI „stundenlang ohne Unterbrechung“ fahren. Alternativ können aber auch andere Open-Source-Tools eingebunden werden. Laut Comma AI benötigen Fahrer:innen nur die Hardware selbst, die für knapp 1.000 US-Dollar erhältlich ist.
In den sozialen Medien wie X feiern erste User:innen von Comma AI das Gadget als Befreiung von den proprietären Systemen von Tesla und Co. Ein User zeigt etwa ein Zeitraffervideo vom Einsatz des Comma Four in einem Tesla Model Y. Statt Elon Musks Unternehmen für das autonome Fahren monatlich zu bezahlen, setzt er auf den Einmalkauf und offene Modelle für autonomes Fahren.
Diese Risiken stecken im FSD-Gadget
In den USA hat das Gadget von Comma AI allerdings nicht nur Käufer:innen, sondern auch die Behörden auf den Plan gerufen. Wie Futurism berichtet, hat die National Highway Transportation Safety Administration eine Untersuchung des Unternehmens angestoßen. Darin geht es um insgesamt fünf Unfälle, bei denen Fahrzeuge mit Comma-Gadget und Openpilot von hinten gegen langsamere oder parkende Autos in ihrer Spur gefahren sind. Bei diesen Unfällen gab es drei Todesfälle.
Teil der Untersuchungen ist ebenfalls das Werbeversprechen von Comma AI. Darin heißt es, dass Kund:innen ihr Fahrzeug ganz ohne Hände fahren könnten. Erst im Kleingedruckten steht, dass sie jederzeit die Aktionen des Comma-Gadgets überwachen müssen. Und auch unter den Videos auf Social Media sammeln sich besorgte Stimmen zu dem Gadget und denjenigen, die es im Straßenverkehr nutzen.
Da Nutzer:innen des Comma Four die freie Softwarewahl haben, besteht die Gefahr, dass sie experimentelle Open-Source-Projekte auf der Straße nutzen. Ein X-User schrieb zu dem Clip: „Stell dir vor, du fährst mit deiner Familie nach Hause und dein Typ fährt in dich hinein, weil er einen Pull-Request von GitHub nutzt, der 2.000 Sternebewertungen hat und per Vibe-Coding erstellt wurde.“ Ein anderer schreibt dazu: „Ich denke nicht, dass wir Menschen jede Software auf der Straße nutzen lassen sollten, die sie nutzen wollen. Das ist nicht Skyrim für Linux. Man bekommt keine Mods auf der Autobahn.“

articles.title: Egyptian fintech startup Paymob raises $35m pre-Series C funding round - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Egyptian startup Paymob, the leading payments infrastructure service provider in the MENA region, has secured US$35 million in a pre-Series C funding round to support its ongoing expansion across the region.
Founded in 2015 by Islam Shawky, Alain El Hajj and Mostafa Menessy, Paymob is an infrastructure technology enabler providing payment solutions to empower digital financial service providers through mobile wallet technology.
Its omnichannel gateway offers more than 60 payment solutions and empowers close to 350,000 merchants with access to innovative financial services. It has expanded to the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Saudi Arabia and Oman.
Disrupt Africa reported in September 2024 Paymob had extended its Series B round to US$72 million, and it has now secured US$35 million in pre-Series C funding in a round co-led by Mubadala Investment Company, an Abu Dhabi-based sovereign investor, and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). British International Investment, Global Ventures and DPI Ventures also took part in the raise.
The fresh capital will support Paymob’s ongoing growth across MENA, by scaling its core digital payments acceptance operations and by rolling out new products aimed at SME merchants and at agentic commerce use cases. Paymob has onboarded around 20,000 merchants across its three GCC markets since it received its Retail Payment Services Licence from the Central Bank of the UAE in January 2025.
“Paymob morphed into a regional platform over the past 18 months, propelled by the exponential growth of our GCC business. This pre-Series C funding round will help us accelerate our growth plan across the MENA region and fast-track our product roadmap to become the go-to payments platform for agentic commerce. We are very excited about Mubadala joining our cap table and grateful for the continued support of our existing shareholders,” Shawky, Paymob’s CEO, said.

articles.title: Not unicorns, lifelines: 5 Northeast startups building for problems they grew up with
articles.text:
Not unicorns, lifelines: 5 Northeast startups building for problems they grew up with
Meet five Northeast startups building solutions for electricity, healthcare, water, language and accessibility challenges across the region.
From villages without reliable electricity to AI that understands Northeast Indian languages, a new generation of founders is building technology around problems they have seen up close.
The founders who gathered in Sikkim last weekend for AIC-SMUTBI's Entrepreneurship and Innovation Convergence were not just talking about markets and valuations. Across two days at Sikkim Manipal Institute of Technology in Majitar, startups, investors, policymakers and academics from all eight Northeastern states discussed how technology can address challenges that remain deeply local.
The gathering included the Digi SAPNE 2.0 Demo Day, the North East Entrepreneurs Dialogue (N.E.E.D '26) and the fourth edition of the Entrepreneurs' Meet.
YourStory Founder and CEO Shraddha Sharma met several founders from across the region. Their companies are working on problems around electricity, healthcare infrastructure, clean water, language access and assistive technology.
Tej Chingtham of AIC-SMUTBI captured one of the larger challenges in a line that stayed with the room: the Northeast needs more “adventure capitalists”, not just venture capitalists.
Here are five startups building from that starting point.
Kiita Dumbang Mountain Winds: Making energy more local
Founder: Mem Modi | Arunachal Pradesh
Kiita Dumbang is a tree on the trail between Mariyang and Paki Modi in Upper Siang. It is also the name behind Mem Modi's company, rooted in her ancestral home in Paki Modi, where reliable electricity remains a challenge.
Kiita Dumbang Mountain Winds began with small Vertical Axis Wind Turbine systems designed for low-wind, remote and hilly areas. Field experience exposed another problem: when equipment fails in a remote village, spare parts and technical expertise can be hundreds of kilometres away.
The startup is now developing a decentralised renewable energy intelligence platform combining small hydro, wind, solar, battery storage, IoT and AI-based monitoring.
For Modi, decentralisation is not only about generating power locally. It also means building local knowledge, maintenance capabilities and eventually manufacturing capacity.
The company is currently part of an 18-month incubation programme at PIEDS, with access to mentorship, technical credits, workspace and funding opportunities.
Labdig: Putting a microscope in a smartphone
Founders: Dr Chayanika Deka Nath and Dr Pabitra Nath | Assam
For many schools, healthcare facilities and field workers, access to laboratory infrastructure can be difficult. Labdig Innovations and Systems is trying to reduce that dependency with Moboscope, a portable smartphone-based microscopy system.
Founded in 2022, Labdig is the first deeptech startup to emerge from Tezpur University. Moboscope was developed from research at the university's Applied Photonics and Nanophotonics Laboratory and officially launched in May 2026.
The system is designed to work without external power or specialised laboratory infrastructure. It can be used for scientific education as well as applications in healthcare, agriculture and field settings.
HN Technovations: Turning floodwater into drinking water
Founder: Prof Harjeet Nath | Tripura
Floods create a strange contradiction in the Northeast: water can be everywhere while safe drinking water becomes difficult to access.
That problem led Harjeet Nath to develop HN Technovations at Tripura Central University's Department of Chemical and Polymer Engineering. Its InstaWater systems treat contaminated water at the point of use rather than relying on bottled water supplies.
During this year's monsoon, the startup supplied more than 2,000 litres of purified water to around 30 flood-affected families in Assam's Amguri and nearby areas.
Its portfolio includes 3kg rechargeable units, petrol-pump-operated systems treating 250–300 litres per hour, and solar-hybrid smart filters with digital TDS monitoring. Across Assam, Tripura and Punjab, InstaWater says its deployments have delivered more than 50,000 litres of clean drinking water since 2019, serving over 3,500 families and preventing around 12,000kg of plastic bottle waste.
MWire Labs: Building AI for Northeast languages
Founder: Badal Nyalang | Meghalaya
Language is another infrastructure gap. MWire Labs, based in Shillong, is building AI systems for the region's low-resource languages, where digital datasets and language technology remain limited.
Its NE-BERT model was trained on 8.3 million sentences covering nine Northeast Indian languages, alongside Hindi and English.
The research found that NE-BERT recorded the lowest average perplexity across all nine languages compared with IndicBERT-V2, MuRIL and mBERT, with particularly strong results for lower-resource languages such as Pnar, Kokborok, Garo and Nyishi.
The company has also developed Lemka, a speech-AI system designed for six Northeast languages, including Kokborok. It is built for local-language interaction in settings where typing, reading or reliable connectivity can be a barrier.
Akumen AI: Making assistive technology more accessible
Founder: Thiyam Akuvan | Manipur
For people with visual impairments, everyday tasks can become harder when assistive devices are expensive or difficult to access. Imphal-based Akumen AI is developing locally built technology to address that gap.
Founded in 2021, the company is developing INSIGHT, an AI-enabled wearable designed to read text, identify objects and faces, recognise currencies and provide audio assistance. The company says the device is being developed with support for 22 Indian languages, including Manipuri.
Akumen's stated focus is to make assistive technology more affordable while using AI, computer vision and other technologies to support people with disabilities.
Why these startups matter
What connects these companies is not a single technology or sector. It is the starting point.
The founders are building around constraints they have encountered in their own communities: limited electricity, scarce laboratory infrastructure, difficult access to safe water, low-resource languages and expensive assistive devices.
That gives their work a different relationship with the problems they are trying to solve. But turning locally grounded solutions into sustainable businesses will require more than early-stage innovation. They will need patient capital, customers beyond their immediate markets, technical partnerships and continued access to infrastructure and expertise.
That is where the Northeast's startup ecosystem will be tested next. As Tej Chingtham put it, the region needs more “adventure capitalists” willing to back founders building for difficult markets.

articles.title: Bitget hacked via zero-day in third-party security products
articles.text:
Cryptocurrency exchange Bitget revealed today that attackers who stole $387.5 million last week breached its systems after exploiting a zero-day flaw in third-party security products.
According to Bitget, two separate investigations by blockchain security firm SlowMist and Google Cloud's cyber-defense arm Mandiant said the threat actors accessed Bitget's wallet environment after compromising two security appliances with zero-day exploits.
After the breach, the attackers dropped web shells on one of the hacked appliances and malware on the crypto exchange's production wallet job server, as well as a custom withdrawal tool used to launch the cryptocurrency theft after midnight on September 25.
"The earliest malicious activity identified in the available logs dates to August 31. A service running on one of Product A's nodes was affected by a zero-day vulnerability. The attacker ran a hidden script under the service process, launched a command to read the environment variable containing the database password, and connected to the database. Similar hidden-script activity was observed on two other nodes on September 23 and September 25," SlowMist said.
"Forensic findings indicate that on September 24, 2026, a threat actor gained unauthorised privileged access to Bitget's third party security appliances A and B. The threat actor deployed a web shell onto the security appliance B and established a Command-and-Control (C2) connection. Using the persistent access on security appliance B, the threat actor moved laterally to Bitget's production wallet job server and deployed malicious packages," Mandiant added.
SlowMist added that the earliest crypto theft transfer occurred on September 02:31 (UTC+8) and the last took place at 05:23, with the attack spanning nearly 3 hours across multiple blockchains.
Bitget suspended all withdrawals on Thursday after detecting multiple unauthorized transfers from its hot and warm crypto wallets and discovering that attackers had stolen $387.5 million from them.
CEO Gracy Chen noted the incident affected multiple assets, including ETH, XRP, BNB, AVAX, USDT, USDC, and other tokens, and involved the Ethereum, XRP Ledger, Arbitrum, Avalanche, Optimism, BSC, and Base chains.
Chen also blamed the attack on North Korean hackers, citing IP behavior patterns and on-chain analysis as evidence, and added that they breached a critical backend system within Bitget's wallet infrastructure that was later used to spoof transaction data, triggering the exchange's authorization process to move funds out of compromised hot/warm wallets.
North Korean hackers have been behind many other major crypto heists, including the Bybit hack, in which they stole $1.5 billion from the crypto exchange's ETH cold wallet.
Since the breach, Bitget has launched a Recovery Bounty Program that offers bounties of 5% to those who help recover or freeze funds stolen in the attack.
A Bitget spokesperson was not immediately available when BleepingComputer contacted them earlier today for more information on the zero-day flaw and the third-party security products compromised in the attack.

articles.title: Se buscan voluntarios para vivir gratis en un refugio de la Sierra de Gredos a cambio de trabajar 24 horas semanales cuidando animales abandonados
articles.text:
¿Alguien se acuerda de ‘Perdidos’ (‘Lost’, 2004-2010)? En la mítica serie, la Iniciativa Dharma era un proyecto científico con estación zoológica propia, la Hidra, donde había osos polares enjaulados que, según los creadores de la serie, escaparon cuando la base cayó. En la Sierra de Gredos (en el término entre Cáceres y Toledo) hay otro Dharma. Pero este santuario hace lo contrario: busca voluntarios para cuidar a más de 100 animales rescatados, 4 horas al día durante 6 días, a cambio de habitación compartida, pensión completa, lavandería, internet y transporte desde el punto de llegada.
Son 24 horas semanales, el 60% de una jornada completa de 40. El proyecto asegura haber rescatado más de 200 animales desde sus inicios y hoy alberga a más de un centenar de 12 especies, desde perros, gatos y caballos hasta cerdos vietnamitas, ocas y hasta una suricata, en 14 hectáreas junto al Tiétar. Además, siguen un régimen de consumo energético responsable.
Tres turnos y un día libre. Por la mañana se abren las casetas, se cuentan los animales, se revisa su salud, se les da de comer y se limpia. Por la tarde se refuerza la alimentación y se comprueban los bebederos. Al anochecer se les da la cena y se les resguarda. Como el proyecto sigue en construcción, también toca levantar vallas o arreglar establos. Hay un día completo de descanso a la semana. El proyecto, por cierto, también cuenta con su propia tienda de merchandising, alimento orgánico e incluso transportines para gatos y perros.
Lo que el "gratis" no incluye. El santuario pide veganismo durante la estancia, mayoría de edad, buen español y transporte propio, y prohíbe tabaco, vapeadores, alcohol, drogas y mascotas. Varios medios dicen que tampoco acepta parejas, pero su ficha en Worldpackers admite solos, parejas y dúos. Hay tres modalidades (estancia larga, corta o simple visita) y dos vías de solicitud: el formulario o Worldpackers. La plataforma cobra a los voluntarios una membresía anual de unos 59 dólares para viajeros individuales.
¿Voluntariado o empleo sin nómina? La Ley 45/2015 exige que el voluntariado sea solidario y libre, sin contraprestación económica o material más allá de gastos reembolsables, y canalizado por una entidad de voluntariado. Pide acuerdo por escrito (art. 12) y seguro de accidente y enfermedad a cargo de la entidad (art. 10). En caso de duda, siempre puedes escribirles a santuariodharma@gmail.com.
¿Cuál es la frontera con un empleo normal y corriente? Según el blog laboral de Garrigues, el horario no basta para distinguirlo: pesa la contraprestación. El TSJ de Castilla y León (9 de marzo de 2016) no vio salario en el alojamiento y la manutención de unos monitores de campamento. Otro TSJ, el andaluz, declaró laboral la relación de unos socorristas que cobraban 40 euros por jornada de 8 horas. Como vara de medir, a prorrata del SMI de 2026, 24 horas semanales serían unos 733 euros brutos al mes en 14 pagas.
Por qué veganos. Porque es de lógica. Desde la Ley 17/2021, el Código Civil reconoce a los animales como seres vivos dotados de sensibilidad. La Ley 7/2023 de bienestar animal, en cambio, deja fuera a los animales de producción (cerdos, cabras, gallinas), salvo que, al perder su fin "productivo", el titular los inscriba como animales de compañía, y a la fauna silvestre en libertad. Para un santuario que acoge animales de granja, la distinción es clave. Dharma dice ofrecer atención veterinaria y un hogar seguro a animales maltratados o abandonados, y promueve el veganismo y la empatía hacia todos los animales.
Por qué faltan manos. En 2025 ingresaron en centros de acogida 285.720 animales de compañía, 169.268 perros y 116.452 gatos. Solo el 42,9% de los perros y el 41,9% de los gatos encontraron hogar, y el 39% de las entidades no contaban con empleos remunerados. La Dirección General de Animales admite que no existe estadística oficial. Es más, estas cifras cubren perros y gatos, no los cerdos, caballos o cabras que acoge Dharma. Recuerda: abandonar a un animal es infracción grave según la Ley 7/2023, con multas de 10.000 a 50.000 euros.
No es la única oferta de este tipo. SEO/BirdLife todavía busca voluntarios para vivir diez días, del 6 al 15 de noviembre, en la finca toledana de Quintos de Mora. Ofrece alojamiento, manutención, material y seguro de accidentes, y su programa recibe cerca de 1.000 solicitudes al año. En la España rural, además, los anuncios de "casa gratis" suelen esconder letra pequeña, así que mejor leerlo todo bien. Antes de hacer la maleta conviene pedir por escrito qué funciones, cuántas horas y qué gastos cubre el acuerdo, y quién asegura al voluntario.

articles.title: How Dangote’s IPO exposed Africa’s digital investing limits
articles.text:
A Zimbabwean investor looking to buy shares in Dangote Refinery’s $1.6 billion initial public offering (IPO) cannot simply open an app and tap “invest”. The offer is structured primarily for investors in Nigeria, leaving Zimbabweans without the same direct route available to domestic investors.
Bard Santner Investors (BSI), the Zimbabwean asset manager facilitating local participation, has created a permitted cross-border route for Zimbabweans to access the offer. It must secure regulatory approvals, process funds and route applications through Ecobank’s cross-border banking and nominee arrangements.
The problem in Nigeria was app capacity; for Zimbabwean investors, it is the cross-border process. When the IPO opened on September 14, Bamboo and Cowrywise struggled with a surge in traffic, exposing capacity constraints and dependencies on third-party services. Zimbabwean investors face a different set of hurdles: manual approvals, cross-border bank transfers and nominee arrangements required to invest from outside Nigeria.
Together, the experiences expose a challenge for Africa’s expanding retail-investment market: digital platforms are widening access to capital markets, but the systems behind them are not always prepared for demand or cross-border complexity. The outages exposed how quickly investor demand can overwhelm digital investment services.
“So far, because of the time, we couldn’t do online applications. We are doing it more manually,” Ngoni Chikowore, head of asset management at Bard Santner, told TechCabal in an interview on Wednesday.
Chikowore said the transaction is treated as an offshore investment in both Nigeria and Zimbabwe, requiring exchange-control approval and supporting documentation. BSI then transfers client funds through Ecobank Zimbabwe to Ecobank Nigeria, where Ecobank Nominees submits the IPO application on the firm’s behalf.
The arrangement gives Zimbabweans a route into the offer, but shows how cross-border investing still depends on intermediaries, regulatory processes and bank transfers. BSI’s minimum investment is $20,000, reflecting the requirements of its route for eligible African investors, rather than the much smaller minimum available to domestic Nigerian applicants.
The Nigerian disruption mattered beyond the country’s borders. Chikowore said it did not ultimately derail BSI’s process because funds moved through the banking system, and the firm retained evidence of participation. But he identified a potential risk before the share allotment, when applications and funds were still moving through the process.
“The only risk is if maybe before allotment,” he said. “When we transfer the funds, we are transferring them through the banking sector through Ecobank Zimbabwe to Ecobank Nigeria, so we have evidence or a claim to say we have participated.”
Bamboo said it added more than 236,000 accounts in the week before the IPO, of which 152,000 were funded and trading. Cowrywise’s service was slow for about an hour before being restored.
Richmond Bassey, Bamboo’s chief executive, told Nairametrics on September 24 that traffic rose to more than 10 times normal levels in the first 30 minutes. The company had expected four to five times normal traffic and had prepared capacity for up to 10 times that.
Bassey said critical processes relied on third-party providers, including one-time passwords, account creation, password resets, deposits and know-your-customer checks. Delays and repeated attempts added pressure, while Cloudflare throttled traffic. His account pointed to capacity and dependency problems, rather than a reported cyberattack or security breach.
An app outage does not prove that an entire financial system has failed. But it shows how an investment experience depends on a chain of services, any of which may become a bottleneck during a sudden surge. Adding users is not the same as ensuring that the entire transaction journey can accommodate them.
Dangote’s offer is a high-profile test because it is being marketed to investors across Africa. The IPO comprises 4.1 billion shares priced at ₦525 (about $0.40) each, with the offer scheduled to close on October 13 and listing expected in November.
But the wider African market remains relatively shallow. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD) Africa Capital Markets Report 2025 counted 1,141 listed companies across African exchanges, compared with roughly 44,000 globally. African companies accounted for about 1% of global equity capital raised since 2000, while South Africa, Morocco and Egypt represented 80% of the continent’s market capitalisation.
That makes the push to bring more retail investors into African capital markets particularly significant and piles greater pressure on the digital and financial infrastructure connecting them.
Nigerian retail investors can apply through digital platforms, while Zimbabweans using BSI must navigate approvals and a manual process the firm hopes to automate as part of its long-term plans. Digital access is expanding, but the practical ability to invest still depends on geography, regulation and the infrastructure connecting markets.
Regional initiatives such as the African Exchanges Linkage Project and the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System aim to improve market connectivity and payment systems. But they do not remove the need for individual platforms to test capacity, manage third-party dependencies and communicate clearly during disruptions.
The Dangote IPO shows both the promise and limits of digital investment. Platforms can bring more people to capital markets, while intermediaries can create routes for investors who cannot access an offer directly. But the next stage of growth requires more than onboarding campaigns and app interfaces.
For retail investing to scale across borders, systems must be resilient enough to handle demand, and processes connecting investors, banks, brokers and exchanges must be dependable. Otherwise, broader participation will remain easier to advertise than to deliver.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Government, Finance Orgs Targeted in Weeks-Long NetScaler Zero-Day Attacks
articles.text:
Google’s Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) have published details on attacks exploiting the NetScaler zero-days that Citrix patched over the weekend.
The vulnerabilities are tracked as CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, and they affect NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway instances. Attackers can exploit these critical flaws for unauthenticated remote code execution.
Before Citrix released patches, government cybersecurity agencies and security firms took the rare step of urging administrators to disconnect affected NetScaler appliances from the internet immediately while zero-day exploitation investigations were ongoing.
Mandiant and GTIG, whose report focuses on the exploitation of CVE-2026-88772, spotted attacks in late September. However, their investigation found that the zero-day campaign has been “ongoing since at least early September.”
The attacks likely impacted organizations in North America and Europe. These organizations are in the government, financial services, education, legal, and professional services sectors.
The attackers exploited the vulnerability to gain root access to NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances. They then changed the appliance’s web server configuration so they could plant web shells and run them with root privileges.
Mandiant found previously unseen malware in the attacks, including a PHP web shell named WHIPSHOT and a Python-based tunneling tool named SLAPSHOT. The two work together to give the attackers a path from the compromised appliance into the victim’s internal network.
According to Mandiant, the tools enable internal reconnaissance, lateral movement and credential theft. In at least one intrusion, the hackers used the tunnel to manually explore the internal network and steal credentials.
Mandiant also saw signs that the threat actor may be managing similar web shells in multiple compromised environments.
Mandiant CTO Charles Carmakal noted that dozens of organizations have been hit, including by suspected state-sponsored threat actors.
“We expect broad and opportunistic exploitation of CVE-2026-88772 and CVE-2026-88771 by a variety of threat actors in the near term,” Carmakal warned.
Cybersecurity expert Kevin Beaumont reported being aware of more than 100 victim organizations as of Tuesday, noting that the attacks appear to be part of an espionage campaign.
Security firm WatchTowr, one of the first to confirm in-the-wild exploitation, has released technical details on both CVE-2026-88772 and CVE-2026-88771.
Threat intelligence company GreyNoise observed zero-day exploitation attempts on September 24, several days before the flaws were disclosed and patched.
“The [malicious cyber actor] attempted to set both the Set User ID (setuid) and Set Group ID (setgid) bits on /bin/sh to obtain a root shell and install a password-protected webshell that accepts communication by the cookie value sent by the adversary. This may be to avoid persisting their commands in web logs,” GreyNoise explained.
Palo Alto Networks reported that there had been roughly 50,000 potentially exposed NetScaler instances as of September 27.
Related: Microsoft SharePoint Flaw CVE-2026-65660 Now Exploited in Attacks
Related: Apple Patches Zero-Day Linked to ‘Extremely Sophisticated Attack’

articles.title: La transition électrique repoussée : Bentley jette l'éponge pour ses prochains projets
articles.text:
Avec le nouveau Torcal, on pensait Bentley fin prêt à aborder le virage électrique avec toute une ribambelle de modèles à batterie. En reprenant les soubassements du Porsche Cayenne, le SUV anglais partait en effet sur de bonnes bases avec 888 ch, 1 350 Nm de couple et un 0 à 100 km/h en 2,8 secondes. La batterie de 113 kWh assurait même une confortable autonomie dépassant les 600 km et une recharge pouvant tutoyer les 400 kW en courant continu DC.
Un beau début qui n’enfantera pour le moment aucun autre véhicule électrique, du moins pas avant 2030. Le revirement est brutal, car Bentley avait initialement prévu de remplacer dès 2020 ses modèles existants par des véhicules électriques sans exception. Le but était alors de passer entièrement aux voitures à batterie en 2030. Un objectif aujourd’hui évaporé en raison de l’incertitude générale planant sur l’industrie automobile.
Pourquoi la stratégie de Bentley vole en éclats
Dans une interview accordée à Autocar, Frank-Steffan Walliser, le PDG de Bentley, explique qu’ « avec tous les préparatifs et les changements constants – et je suis sûr que les organismes de réglementation ont de nouvelles idées chaque semaine – ma réponse n’est peut-être pas celle que vous attendez : nous allons introduire plus de flexibilité dans nos stratégies ». En d’autres termes, les plans futurs ne sont désormais plus gravés dans le marbre.
Vu que le contexte est particulièrement instable avec une baisse notable de la demande en véhicules électriques de luxe, l’adaptabilité est devenue le maître mot pour les constructeurs comme Bentley. Walliser affirme que sa marque essaiera « de réunir à l’avenir les véhicules électriques et les hybrides rechargeables sur la même ligne, afin d’avoir une flexibilité totale – notamment pour répondre à la demande du marché et aux réglementations ».
Le thermique et l’hybride jouent les prolongations
Pour réagir au mieux aux éventuels changements, Bentley a réduit les délais de conception de ses nouveaux modèles à 48 mois. Bien, mais encore insuffisant, l’objectif final étant de compresser ce temps à seulement 36 mois en se calquant sur ce que fait Volkswagen. Cela signifie donc que le thermique n’est pas mort et fera encore des heures supplémentaires par l’hybridation.
Vient alors une question : le Torcal pourrait-il avoir droit à une version hybride ? Non, répond Walliser, car le SUV est basé sur une plateforme uniquement dédiée aux motorisations électriques. Faire une adaptation hybride engendrerait des frais trop importants et menacerait en parallèle le Bentayga, à peine plus grand et bénéficiant déjà d’une déclinaison hybride. Cela dit, de futurs modèles multi énergies ne sont plus à exclure.

articles.title: Votre VPN ne fonctionne plus ? Voici les vérifications à faire avant de changer
articles.text:
VPN ne fonctionne plus : les vérifications à faire avant de changer d’abonnement
Un VPN qui ralentit, refuse la connexion ou bloque certains sites n’est pas forcément défectueux. Voici les vérifications à effectuer avant de changer de fournisseur.
Un VPN qui refuse de se connecter, ralentit fortement Internet ou empêche l'accès à certains sites n'est pas forcément défectueux. Le problème peut venir du serveur choisi, du réseau utilisé, du protocole de connexion ou encore du service consulté. Avant de résilier son abonnement, quelques vérifications permettent généralement d'identifier l'origine du problème.
Pourquoi un VPN peut-il ne plus fonctionner ?
Avec un VPN, la connexion passe d’abord par un serveur avant de rejoindre Internet. L’adresse IP est ainsi masquée, tandis que les données échangées entre l’appareil et le serveur sont chiffrées.
Cette étape supplémentaire peut cependant créer de nouveaux points de blocage. Un serveur peut être momentanément saturé, une connexion peut être mal établie ou un réseau peut limiter certains protocoles VPN. Dans d'autres cas, c'est le site ou l'application utilisé qui refuse l'adresse IP du serveur.
Le premier réflexe consiste donc à déterminer si le problème vient réellement du VPN. Si Internet fonctionne normalement dès que la connexion VPN est désactivée, cela donne déjà une première indication. À l'inverse, si la connexion reste lente ou instable sans VPN, le problème se situe probablement ailleurs.
Le serveur choisi peut être en cause
Même chez un même fournisseur, tous les serveurs ne se valent pas. La distance avec le serveur, le nombre de personnes qui y sont connectées ou encore l’adresse IP utilisée peuvent parfois expliquer une connexion plus lente ou moins stable.
Un serveur situé dans un pays très éloigné peut ainsi entraîner davantage de latence. Pour une navigation classique, la différence reste parfois peu visible. Elle peut en revanche devenir plus gênante lors d'un appel vidéo, d'un jeu en ligne ou d'un transfert de fichiers.
La solution la plus simple consiste alors à changer de localisation. Si un autre serveur fonctionne correctement, il n'est pas nécessaire de remettre immédiatement en question l'abonnement.
Le réseau utilisé peut également bloquer le VPN
Le problème peut aussi apparaître uniquement sur certains réseaux. Un Wi-Fi public, un réseau d'entreprise ou une connexion particulièrement restrictive peut empêcher l'établissement d'un tunnel VPN.
Un test sur un autre réseau permet de vérifier rapidement cette hypothèse. Si le VPN fonctionne avec une connexion mobile mais pas sur le Wi-Fi habituel, le fournisseur VPN n'est probablement pas le seul responsable.
Certains sites peuvent refuser les adresses IP de VPN
Les services en ligne sont également capables d'identifier certaines adresses IP associées à des VPN. Ils peuvent alors demander une vérification supplémentaire, limiter l'accès ou refuser la connexion.
Le problème ne signifie pas forcément que le VPN est inutilisable. Changer de serveur peut suffire lorsque plusieurs adresses IP sont disponibles. En revanche, si un service bloque systématiquement les connexions provenant de VPN, changer de fournisseur n'apportera pas nécessairement une solution durable.
Les vérifications à faire avant de changer d'abonnement
Avant de résilier un abonnement, quelques manipulations simples permettent de cerner le problème.
1. Tester un autre serveur
C'est généralement le premier test à effectuer. Il permet de vérifier si le problème est lié à une localisation précise.
Si la vitesse compte, mieux vaut privilégier un serveur situé à proximité. Plus il est éloigné, plus la latence risque d’augmenter, ce qui peut se ressentir lors de la navigation ou des activités qui demandent une connexion réactive.
2. Comparer avec et sans VPN
Désactiver temporairement le VPN permet de savoir si la connexion Internet elle-même fonctionne correctement.
Si les pages restent lentes sans VPN, il faut plutôt rechercher une cause du côté de la connexion, du routeur ou du fournisseur d'accès. Si tout redevient normal dès que le VPN est coupé, les tests peuvent se poursuivre du côté de l'application VPN.
3. Essayer un autre protocole
Les applications VPN proposent souvent plusieurs protocoles de connexion. Leur comportement peut varier selon le réseau utilisé.
Lorsqu'une connexion refuse de s'établir ou devient instable, changer de protocole peut donc être pertinent. Il n'est pas nécessaire de modifier plusieurs réglages simultanément : mieux vaut procéder étape par étape afin de savoir ce qui a réellement corrigé le problème.
4. Redémarrer l'application
Cela paraît basique, mais fermer complètement l'application VPN puis la relancer peut résoudre certains problèmes temporaires. Un redémarrage de l'appareil peut également être utile lorsque la connexion réseau semble bloquée.
Il faut aussi vérifier que l'application et le système d'exploitation disposent de leurs dernières mises à jour. Une ancienne version peut parfois provoquer des incompatibilités avec le réseau ou certaines fonctions du service.
5. Vérifier si le problème concerne un seul service
Un VPN qui fonctionne correctement pour la navigation mais rencontre des difficultés avec une seule plateforme n'est pas forcément en panne.
Il est donc utile de tester plusieurs sites ou applications. Si un seul service refuse la connexion, le blocage peut être spécifique à celui-ci.
Cinq VPN à connaître selon les usages
Les problèmes de connexion ne touchent pas nécessairement un service en particulier. Les principaux VPN proposent toutefois des approches différentes, ce qui peut être intéressant à prendre en compte avant de changer d'abonnement.
NordVPN : pour un usage polyvalent
NordVPN se distingue notamment par l'étendue de son réseau et par le nombre de fonctionnalités proposées. Pour un usage régulier, cette diversité permet de disposer de plusieurs options lorsque certains serveurs rencontrent des difficultés.
Pour la navigation quotidienne, le streaming ou les déplacements, pouvoir essayer différentes localisations peut aussi faciliter le dépannage lorsqu'une connexion devient instable.
Proton VPN : pour privilégier la confidentialité
Proton VPN met davantage l'accent sur la confidentialité.Son offre comprend notamment une formule gratuite, tandis que les abonnements payants donnent accès à davantage de serveurs et de fonctionnalités.
Il peut donc intéresser les utilisateurs qui souhaitent avant tout renforcer la confidentialité de leur connexion, sans forcément rechercher une multitude de réglages.
CyberGhost : pour une prise en main simple
CyberGhost mise sur une interface relativement accessible et un large choix de serveurs. Il peut ainsi convenir aux utilisateurs qui souhaitent sélectionner facilement une localisation sans multiplier les réglages.
Cette simplicité peut être appréciable pour un usage quotidien, notamment lorsqu'il faut simplement activer le VPN ou changer rapidement de serveur.
ExpressVPN : pour rechercher simplicité et performances
ExpressVPN privilégie notamment la simplicité d'utilisation et les performances. Son protocole Lightway est conçu pour établir rapidement une connexion et maintenir une bonne stabilité lors des changements de réseau.
Il peut donc trouver sa place sur un ordinateur portable ou un smartphone régulièrement utilisé sur différents réseaux Wi-Fi et mobiles.
Surfshark : pour plusieurs appareils
Surfshark se démarque surtout par la possibilité de protéger plusieurs appareils avec un même abonnement.Un point intéressant pour les foyers équipés de nombreux smartphones, ordinateurs ou tablettes.
L'intérêt est ici moins lié à un usage particulier qu'à la possibilité de retrouver une protection VPN sur plusieurs appareils sans multiplier les abonnements.
Au final, ces différences ne permettent pas de désigner un VPN systématiquement épargné par les problèmes de connexion. Un blocage peut dépendre du serveur, du réseau ou du service consulté, même avec un VPN réputé.
Quand faut-il vraiment changer de VPN ?
Changer de fournisseur peut devenir pertinent lorsque les problèmes sont fréquents et persistent malgré les différents tests. C'est notamment le cas si plusieurs serveurs sont régulièrement inutilisables, si les déconnexions se répètent sur différents réseaux ou si l'application présente des problèmes récurrents.
Le support client peut également être sollicité avant de résilier. Le fournisseur est parfois en mesure d'identifier une panne connue ou de proposer une configuration adaptée au réseau utilisé.
Il faut surtout éviter de conclure trop rapidement qu'un VPN est mauvais parce qu'une seule connexion ne fonctionne pas. Un problème isolé sur un serveur ou avec une plateforme ne suffit pas à juger l'ensemble du service.
Avant de changer d'abonnement VPN, mieux vaut donc chercher l'origine du problème. Tester plusieurs serveurs, comparer la connexion avec et sans VPN, essayer un autre protocole et vérifier le comportement sur différents services permet déjà d'écarter de nombreuses causes.
Si les difficultés persistent malgré ces vérifications, un changement de fournisseur peut alors avoir du sens. Mais dans de nombreux cas, quelques réglages suffisent à retrouver une connexion normale sans avoir à résilier son abonnement.

articles.title: Swedish micromobility company Voi secures €150 million RCF to redeem outstanding bonds and scale its fleet | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Voi Technology, the Stockholm-based e-scooter and e-bike sharing company, has signed a €150 million revolving credit facility (RCF) with three Nordic banks.
The Swedish micromobility startup has entered into the new RCF (new facility) with Danske Bank, Swedbank and DNB Sweden. According to Voi, this new facility represents a further step in its financial development and marks a new stage in its financing strategy.
“This is an important milestone in our financial development, and follows the strong cash flow generation over the past years. The new facility gives us access to more flexible and cost-efficient financing as we continue to scale. We thank our current banks Danske Bank and Swedbank for their continued support and welcome DNB Bank on our journey ahead,” said Mathias Hermansson, CFO and Deputy CEO of Voi.
Founded in Stockholm in 2018, Voi provides shared electric scooters and e-bikes in partnership with towns and cities across Europe. The company currently operates more than 200k vehicles across more than 130 towns and cities in 13 countries, employs roughly 1,000 people at its Stockholm headquarters, and has recorded more than 500 million rides from over 4 million active users annually.
The new revolving credit facility comes on the back of strong second-quarter results. During Q2 2026, Voi reported net revenue climbed 47% year-on-year to €68.8 million, pushing its trailing twelve-month revenue above €200 million for the first time. The company’s adjusted EBITDA also nearly doubled to €19.7 million, giving it a margin of 28.6%. Voi also reported net leverage fell to 1.76x from 2.41x at the end of the previous quarter, despite its continued investment in fleet expansion.
Voi says it will use the proceeds to redeem all of its outstanding bonds, refinance its existing undrawn credit line and continue expanding its vehicle fleet. As part of the transaction, Voi issued a conditional notice of early redemption for all outstanding bonds under ISIN SE0023134952, which were issued under terms dated 17 October 2024.
The redemption of all outstanding bonds depends on customary conditions for the first drawdown of the new facility being satisfied, and, if met, is expected to close on 19 October 2026. The company also confirmed that bondholders will be repaid at 103.375% of the nominal value of each bond, plus accrued interest, with the payment due to holders registered as of 12 October 2026. Voi said the bonds are expected to be delisted from Nasdaq Stockholm’s corporate bond list around that date.
Fredrik Hjelm, co-founder and CEO of Voi, said, “We are coming off another record quarter, in Q2 2026, in a run of record quarters, and our growth trajectory keeps building. This facility is a clear vote of confidence from some of the Nordic region’s leading banks, and a sign that micromobility has matured into a bankable industry. Looking ahead, we will keep scaling our fleet, deepening our partnerships with cities, and working to create cities made for living.”
Since 2018, Voi Technology has raised more than €500 million across 14 funding rounds, including two Seed, four early-stage, five late-stage, 2 debt, and 1 grant prize. In August 2018, Voi raised a €2.5 million Seed round from VNV Global and went on to raise a €77 million Series B in November 2019, followed by a €132 million Series C in December 2020, which remains its largest funding round.
The Series D followed in December 2021 when the company raised €101.36 million ($115 million) and became a unicorn. However, the company has since shifted from pure equity to debt capital markets, issuing €50 million in senior secured bonds in October 2024, a further €40 million tap issue in October 2025, and a €25 million RCF with Danske Bank and Swedbank in December 2025. The €150 million revolving credit facility announced this week supersedes all the previous debt.
Even after its bonds are redeemed and delisted, the company intends to keep reporting its quarterly financing position alongside sustainability disclosures made under the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive. The company says this measure is its continued commitment to transparency with stakeholders.

articles.title: “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer
articles.text:
“We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer
Mark Chen on what the firm is doing to make its models safe, how a slowdown would work, and why the world is better off with OpenAI in it.
Two months after the bombshell news that a swarm of its agents had broken their containment and hacked into the computers of the AI company Hugging Face, OpenAI is still putting out fires. A steady drip of disclosures about other hacks in the weeks since has kept OpenAI in the spotlight and raised serious questions about the safety of its technology.
Last week brought news of another hack, this time into Australia’s national health-care system. The Australian government says that OpenAI did not notify it of the breach until 84 days after it happened.
But OpenAI insists it is not on the back foot. “I do kind of reject the premise that OpenAI is a company with visible impacts in the world and therefore OpenAI is not training safe and aligned models,” says Mark Chen, the company’s chief research officer.
Chen oversees OpenAI’s research teams. The recent agent hacks were accidents that happened during the testing of experimental models on his watch. In a lot of ways, the buck stops with him.
I sat down with Chen in London last Friday to talk about the fallout from the hacks, what his company is doing about it, and why he thinks things are not as bad as they seem.
Later that same day, OpenAI put out a report detailing yet another incident—the first since the company says it took measures to prevent them—in which its agents once again broke out and accessed the public internet when they were not meant to.
Over the weekend, OpenAI announced that it had paused the training of its latest models. A company spokesperson says: “We will resume only when we’re confident we have additional safeguards and alignments in place. We are working on these now. This is not the first time we’ve paused to take such measures, nor do we expect it to be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance.” OpenAI also says that it is now reviewing logs of agent activity dating back to January 2026 to understand what happened in these hacks.
The way Chen sees it, the Hugging Face incident triggered a welcome course correction for the industry. And he wants you to know that OpenAI is setting an example he hopes other companies will follow. “If you disappeared OpenAI, that would be bad for the world,” he says.
Out of control
Chen claims that the drumbeat of new cases in which OpenAI has lost control of its models reflects a deliberate choice on the company’s part.
“When it comes to the broader sphere of effects of the Hugging Face incident, this is something that we have been aware of and we’re figuring out the process of disclosure,” he says. “We want to make sure we do in-depth investigations before we just put details out there in the open.”
The trouble with this approach is that it gives the impression OpenAI has an ongoing problem that it is failing to fix.
But Chen insists that OpenAI is on it. He says the multiple cases (that we know of so far) in which his company’s agents broke containment and behaved in unexpected and undesirable ways were all part of the same cluster of activity in May and June that led to the Hugging Face hack. In short, you can blame the same few models running under the same flawed testing procedures—models and procedures that OpenAI has since dropped, Chen says.
“It’s not like, you know, Hugging Face happened and we patched that and then something else happened and we patched that,” he adds. “We’re just kind of making sure that we responsibly disclose the full waterfall of what happened.”
At least that was the case before Friday’s announcement that OpenAI’s agents had been caught accessing the internet on September 20, weeks after the company claims to have set up new safeguards. In its defense, OpenAI says the activity was flagged 15 minutes after it started (it took the company more than a week to notice the Hugging Face hack) and that this shows the new systems it has put in place to spot such activity are working.
What’s changed
I want to understand what’s changed inside OpenAI in the aftermath of this summer’s hacks that makes Chen confident his team is now back in control.
“Hugging Face felt like a very serious thing,” he says. “There are so many novel behaviors right there. There were multiple agents collaborating on a message board; they found their way out of OpenAI’s infrastructure. We’ve taken it very seriously. We don’t want this kind of thing to ever happen again.”
The realization for OpenAI, says Chen, was that models need to be watched while they are still being trained, not only once they are deployed: “From that moment on, we have treated the process of training as something that’s not secure,” he says.
OpenAI, like other top AI firms, has systems in place to monitor the behavior of its models. It uses specialized LLMs to monitor its consumer models, keeping tabs on their chains of thought—the scratchpads they use to plan ahead and note down partial results. In theory, if a watcher LLM spots signs of undesirable activity in a model’s chain of thought, it will get flagged to a human.
Typically, models were monitored in this way only once they were deployed. Chen says that OpenAI has now started monitoring all its training runs as well.
“We didn’t have the monitors on in training before. It wasn’t industry practice,” he says. “Now every single thing is put through monitors.” Human reviewers can then assess whether or not flagged agents are behaving as they should: “It’s all triage.”
Chen says that in the last couple of months OpenAI has shifted between 5% and 10% of its vast computing resources away from training new models and toward safety work, especially monitoring.
OpenAI has also fixed some of the processes within the organization itself, establishing clearer lines of communication and quicker handoffs between its research and security teams, he says.
All of which sounds sensible. But given how hard OpenAI sells the capabilities of its technology, why weren’t these systems and procedures in place already? Why did the company not see the hacks coming?
“Even just three or four months ago, when we looked at the behavior of these agents during training, the things that were happening were kind of amusing,” says Chen. “For instance, an agent might, you know, reach out to someone on Slack for help with a task.”
The signs were there, but they were misread. Cute behavior—like asking someone for help—that was rewarded during training reinforced a tendency to seek out shortcuts, a type of behavior that became far more consequential down the line. “I think the big update for us was how quickly that kind of behavior can lead to an impact with a footprint as big as the Hugging Face incident,” says Chen.
According to new reporting by the New York Times yesterday, OpenAI employees warned executives, including the firm’s president, Greg Brockman, months before the Hugging Face hack that its models were not being monitored properly during training.
An OpenAI spokesperson says: “As frontier models have become more capable, we continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster. We know we have more work to do, and we’ve recently slowed development and held back models that don’t meet our safety bar. We continue to make significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, and use real-time monitoring to respond faster to misaligned behavior.”
Race vs. pace
OpenAI’s rivals have taken note. Spurred by the fallout from the incident, the major AI labs—including Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and SpaceXAI—have all called for the pace of development to slow down. But how does that square with fierce international competition and trillion-dollar IPOs?
“We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot and take ourselves far off the frontier—that’s just a horrible strategy,” he says. “I think it’s really about setting a norm. The more that we can set that norm, it’ll be safer for the industry as a whole.”
Coordination across US companies will be hard enough. Establishing global norms is harder still, especially given concerns around AI’s impact on national security. If a global race continues, what then? And what about open-source models from outfits beyond the reach of US regulations?
Chen dropped his upbeat manner for the first time in our conversation: “I do think we have to prepare for a world where, say, six months to a year out, we have open-source models with the capability of the agents behind the Hugging Face incident, but which are deliberately misaligned to go attack infrastructure or create harm in the world.”
What that world needs most, says Chen, is OpenAI. “If you entertain for a moment that OpenAI is one of the companies that cares most about alignment—and I believe this to be true; it can be debated, but I really do think it’s true—then if you disappear OpenAI, that would be bad for the world.”
Existential risks
What about the more extreme claims made by some of his Silicon Valley peers that AI could kill us all—and that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are not doing enough to stop it?
“Researchers are a heterogeneous group of people, you know, with beliefs across the spectrum,” he says.
“Personally, I don’t think we have to be resigned to there being some probability that we’re all going to be existentially at risk. We have agency over this. We are not going to go and deploy models if they truly have that kind of probability of causing a risk to humanity. At a frontier lab, you have the ability to work on alignment to the point that you do not feel like you’re incurring more than epsilon risk to the world in deploying your models.”
(In discussions about levels of risk, the Greek letter epsilon is often used as a mathematical placeholder for an acceptable threshold. Chen doesn’t say what his epsilon would be.)
When tech leaders are asked to justify the downsides of AI, their go-to talking point is that the upsides—from helping cure diseases to coming up with cleaner sources of energy—far outweigh the immediate costs. Short-term pains, long-term gains.
But as the downsides pile up, does that case get harder to make? Is there a point where Chen would feel less as if he’s building something amazing and more as if he’s simply minimizing harm—fighting fires rather than forging a better future?
The capabilities of these models are already evident, he says: “It is time to start delivering the benefits of AI to humanity. It’s time to start working on deep problems in drug discovery, on materials, on scientific applications that will actually change people’s lives.”
“Yes, there is a bit of risk that we are incurring, but we see all these benefits,” he adds. “I think we should make that less of an abstract thing. If people can really see the upside, I think they’ll believe in it.”

articles.title: "An AI did it" is no defense, says nonprofit suing OpenAI over Hugging Face hack
articles.text:
OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face in July 2026 has spurred a lawsuit demanding that the company stop accessing third-party computer systems and halt AI development practices that can harm the public. The lawsuit was filed by Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST), which said yesterday that the hack in which OpenAI “agents stole credentials, uploaded malicious files, and gained control over key parts of Hugging Face’s internal systems… is unquestionably illegal under California law.”
California’s Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act (CDAFA) prohibits unauthorized access into computer systems, “and it doesn’t matter that a swarm of AI agents carried out this cyberattack. California law makes it clear that it is not a defense ‘that the artificial intelligence autonomously caused the harm,’” the group said.
The lawsuit, filed in San Francisco County Superior Court, said OpenAI also violated California’s Unfair Competition Law (UCL). “OpenAI’s insistence on externalizing the harms of its unsafe decision-making is a fundamentally unfair business practice,” the complaint said, adding that “such risk-taking for private gain at substantial public expense is immoral, unethical, oppressive, unscrupulous, and substantially injurious conduct.”
LASST said it wants “a court order prohibiting OpenAI’s AI agents from accessing third-party computer systems without permission and forbidding OpenAI from continuing to employ unsafe AI development practices that threaten serious harm to the public.” The lawsuit does not ask for any compensatory or punitive damages from OpenAI, requesting only attorneys’ fees.
OpenAI claims lawsuit “completely without merit”
OpenAI said in a statement provided to Ars that “Hugging Face was a serious incident and we’ve taken a series of actions in response to it, but this lawsuit is completely without merit.” Defending its response to the hack, OpenAI noted that it published a technical report and other information about “third-party impact from misaligned models,” slowed development of its AI, and held back the release of a model that doesn’t meet its safety standards.

articles.title: Precio de ethereum, bitcoin y otras principales criptomonedas para este miércoles 30 de septiembre
articles.text:
Las criptomonedas son un activo digital innovador que han experimentado un crecimiento monumental en los últimos tiempos debido a varios elementos que contribuyen a ello, entre ellos que algunos gobiernos hayan decidido darles una oportunidad como moneda de curso legal; no obstante, también han sufrido descalabros que han puesto en duda su viabilidad, como el más reciente episodio conocido como el "criptoinvierno".
Pese a este panorama, cada vez más personas han empezado a adquirir criptomonedas para poder invertir en algo "seguro" y "fiable" tanto a corto como a largo plazo, a pesar de los niveles extremos de inestabilidad que sufre constantemente.
PUBLICIDAD
Sin embargo, invertir o comprar en criptodivisas es más fácil de lo que parece. Hay que recordar que se trata de monedas virtuales, por lo que serán controladas en carteras o monederos que comparten esa particularidad, pues a diferencia del dinero corriente, no tienen un soporte físico.
El precio de las criptomonedas hoy
Esta es la cotización de las criptodivisas más destacadas en este momento.
El Bitcoin, cotiza a 83.297,08 dólares, lo que implicó un cambio de -0,389% en las últimas horas.
La segunda criptomoneda más popular del mercado, Ethereum, ha mostrado un movimiento de -0,258% en las últimas 24 horas, por lo que su valor se ubica en 2.669,81 dólares.
PUBLICIDAD
En el caso de TetherUs, su precio es de 1 dólares, por lo que en el último día tuvo un movimiento de 0,01%.
Por su parte, BNB, tiene un valor de 759,47 dólares, con un cambio de -0,57%, en cambio el Litecoin cotizó a 66.751 dólares, tras una variación de -3.5732224.
Finalmente, el Dogecoin, una de las monedas virtuales que fue impulsada por Elon Musk, tiene un valor de 0,09 dólares tras presentar un cambio de 0% en las últimas 24 horas.
Qué pasa con las criptodivisas
Luego de que en las primeras semanas de mayo del 2022 se viviera el "criptocrash" o "criptoinvierno" que dejaron al descubierto la enorme volatilidad de estas monedas digitales, ha llegado un nuevo periodo de relativa estabilidad.
PUBLICIDAD
Bitcoin, ethereum y BNB han mostrado variaciones "controladas", puesto que no se han disparado los precios como en semanas previas. Por ejemplo, a inicios de agosto, las mencionadas anteriormente tuvieron un cambio menor del 2%.
Por otra parte, algo que esta llamando la atención en el mundo de las criptomonedas es que China está ablandando sus restricciones y podría comenzar a permitir su uso. Específicamente sería Hong Kong en donde este cambio se haría presente.
Sumado a ello, la plataforma de transacciones digitales PayPal anunció su propia stablecoin llamada PayPal USD (PYUSD), que cuenta por el respaldo de depósitos en dólares, bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos a corto plazo y activos equivalentes.
PUBLICIDAD
La compañía ha afirmado en su declaración que permitirá la transferencia de fondos a monederos digitales de terceros y proporcionará detalles sobre cómo integrar su servicio en exchanges centralizados y descentralizados, con el objetivo de ser utilizado en Finanzas Descentralizadas (DeFi, por sus siglas en inglés). Por lo tanto, es muy probable que se utilice ampliamente en la industria Web3.
Su avance en Latinoamérica
Criptomonedas en México: el Banco de México (Banxico) ha determinado que ninguna de las instituciones que participan en el sistema financiero nacional podrá hacer uso o deberá permitir operaciones de ninguna clase a través de este medio de pago.
En territorio mexicano el empresario Ricardo Salinas Pliego, uno de los más ricos del país, ha mostrado interés en las criptomonedas y ha asegurado que varios de sus negocios aceptarán bitcoin en el futuro, incluido su banco; hasta el momento una de sus tiendas más populares ya lo hace.
PUBLICIDAD
Criptomonedas en Perú: el Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCR) ha dejado en claro que su misión no es ser el primero ni el segundo banco central que regule el uso de las criptomonedas, ello debido a la inestabilidad que las caracteriza. Sin embargo, hace días el presidente del (BCR) aseguró que el BCR trabajaba en un proyecto de moneda digital propia.
Criptomonedas en Colombia: en la nación sudamericana hay más de 500 sitios donde es permitido pagar con criptodivisas. Colombia ocupa el puesto 14 entre 26 países de adopción de criptomonedas, según el informe de Finder.
PUBLICIDAD
Criptomonedas en Centroamérica: en el gobierno de El Salvador, el bitcoin, que en septiembre de 2021 se convirtió en moneda de curso legal, ha perdido oficialmente este estatus en este enero del 2025 tras una reforma aprobada por la Asamblea Legislativa del país. Según informó la prensa local, la modificación de la Ley Bitcoin fue impulsada por el gobierno del presidente Nayib Bukele y respaldada por la mayoría oficialista en el órgano legislativo. Este cambio marca el fin de una política que había colocado al país centroamericano en el centro del debate global sobre las criptomonedas.
¿Cómo crear una criptomoneda?
Al momento de crear una criptomoneda es importante primero determinar qué se desea tener: una moneda o un token. La primera usa su propia blockchain, mientras que la segunda se basa en una red preexistente.
PUBLICIDAD
De acuerdo con el sitio de Binance, para crear una criptomoneda se necesita de un gran equipo de desarrolladores y expertos; mientras que para el token sí se requieren conocimientos técnicos pero es posible crearlo en minutos a través del uso de otras blockchains como Ethereum o BNB, que son las más populares.
Los costos de creación, el tiempo requerido y el uso de fuerza de trabajo dependerá de si se opta por hacer una moneda virtual o un token. En éste último caso también se puede usar un código establecido para crear tokens o pagar para usar un servicio de creación de monedas.
PUBLICIDAD
Es importante saber que antes de crear una criptomoneda se debe considerar su utilidad y estado legal.
En el caso de elegir crear una criptomoneda, entonces se debe elegir una blockchain, posteriormente se debe hacer un plan acorde al funcionamiento y la funcionalidad de la blockchain para diseñar los nodos y la interfaz.
PUBLICIDAD
