articles.title: TDB backs 22 projects under Rs 1 lakh Cr RDI Fund, says industrialist Sudhir Mehta
articles.text:
TDB backs 22 projects under Rs 1 lakh Cr RDI Fund, says industrialist Sudhir Mehta
The first cohort comprises 22 projects involving Rs 4,744 crore in R&D and Rs 2,192 crore in funding from the RDI Fund.
Pinnacle Industries founder and chairman Sudhir Mehta took to X on Tuesday and said that after months of reviewing proposals from Indian founders, he is “more optimistic about India's future than at any point.”
As a member of the Technology Development Board's (TDB's) Investment Committee under the Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund, Mehta said the first cohort comprises 22 projects involving Rs 4,744 crore in R&D and Rs 2,192 crore in funding from the RDI Fund.
The RDI Scheme, approved by the Union Cabinet in July 2025 and launched in November, aims to increase private-sector participation in research and development and support the development and commercialisation of indigenous technologies. The scheme has a six-year outlay and focuses on research-driven and deeptech innovations, particularly in strategic technology sectors.
The scheme is being operationalised through a Special Purpose Fund within the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), with funding channelled to Second-Level Fund Managers (SLFMs). TDB and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) have been designated as SLFMs, while the Department of Science and Technology (DST) is the nodal ministry for the scheme.
Mehta said 14 of the 22 projects in the first cohort are startups, while 13 are in deeptech areas including reusable launch vehicles, Earth observation satellites, quantum-secure communication, Indian chip design, drones, robotics and next-generation batteries.
The selected projects are spread across Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Mumbai, Thane, Noida and Pune.
“India's problem was never ideas. It was patient capital,” Mehta said, adding that the RDI Fund offers financing at 3-4% interest for up to 15 years, without collateral or personal guarantees.
“We spend 0.64% of GDP on R&D, and private industry funds only about 36% of it. RDIF changes the math: 3 to 4% interest, up to 15 years, no collateral, no personal guarantees. Evaluation in 8 weeks, money in 12. And every rupee comes with two conditions: IP stays in India, control stays with Indian citizens.”
“After sitting across the table from these founders, I have no doubt. India's top notch deeptech companies are being built right now. The capital is ready. The founders are ready. This decade belongs to Indian deeptech."

articles.title: OpenAI a été pris de court, l'adresse dot.com ne mène pas chez eux
articles.text:
Le 29 septembre 2026 aura été une date importante pour OpenAI. Parmi les nouveautés annoncées lors de son Dev Day, on retrouve Dots, des agents IA « toujours actifs », propulsés par GPT-6 Astra, qui travaillent pour l’utilisateur en continu.
Chaque dot dispose de son propre nom, de son avatar et de son propre ordinateur dans le cloud, sans avoir besoin de la machine de l’utilisateur. Une sorte de Muse version OpenAI, dont l’entreprise de Sam Altman peut d’ores et déjà souffrir de la comparaison.
Un autre acteur a toutefois tiré la couverture à lui. Sur X, plusieurs tweets relaient https://dot.com pour parler du service réservé aux abonnés ChatGPT Pro. Or cette adresse n’envoie pas vers OpenAI.
Que sait-on de dot.com ?
Alors, facétie ou coup prémédité ? Une chose est sûre, l’URL renvoie vers Grok Bot, l’assistant IA de xAI, société d’Elon Musk.
Difficile d’établir avec certitude que la manœuvre est directement menée par l’éditeur de Grok. Le nom de domaine est enregistré depuis 1994 et son titulaire est masqué par un service d’anonymisation. Selon TechCrunch, qui s’appuie sur le WHOIS, l’annuaire public qui recense le titulaire et les dates clés d’un nom de domaine, dot.com a changé de mains en juillet 2026, soit environ deux mois avant le DevDay. La fiche a encore été modifiée le 28 septembre, la veille de la conférence. Un achat en juillet ne prouve pas pour autant que xAI connaissait déjà le nom du produit d’OpenAI.
Certaines sources avancent que le domaine appartient aujourd’hui à xAI, mais aucune confirmation officielle n’a été apportée, ni par l’une ni par l’autre des deux entreprises.

articles.title: Payer à l’étranger avec Wero : un énorme réseau européen se prépare, sans date de lancement — Frandroid
articles.text:
Cinq applications de paiement nationales vont se brancher les unes aux autres. Dans un communiqué commun publié ce mercredi 30 septembre, l’italien Bancomat, l’espagnol Bizum, EPI (la société derrière Wero), le portugais SIBS avec MB WAY et le nordique Vipps MobilePay annoncent la création de l’European Network for Payments (ENP), basée à Madrid. À terme, un utilisateur de Wero devrait pouvoir envoyer de l’argent à un ami espagnol sur Bizum sans que l’un ou l’autre change d’application.
L’ENP découle d’un protocole d’accord signé par les cinq partenaires en février 2026. Chacun en sera actionnaire à parts égales. Ensemble, leurs solutions desservent environ 130 millions d’utilisateurs dans 13 pays qui rassemblent plus de 70 % de la population de l’Union européenne et de la Norvège.
Le réseau reposera sur des standards européens, notamment le paiement instantané de compte à compte : l’argent passe directement d’un compte bancaire à un autre, sans réseau de carte au milieu. Chaque application garde sa marque et son interface.
Entre particuliers d’abord, en magasin plus tard
Le déploiement commencera par les virements entre particuliers d’un pays à l’autre, d’ici la fin de 2026. Les paiements en ligne et en magasin suivront au cours de 2027.
Visa, Mastercard et PayPal dominent justement ces deux usages en Europe. Les dirigeants misent sur la souveraineté : Fernando Rodríguez, directeur général adjoint de Bizum chargé de l’expansion internationale, estime que l’initiative « renforce l’autonomie stratégique de l’Europe ». Kim Fuglsang Kristoffersen, responsable de la stratégie des paiements chez Vipps MobilePay, veut « une alternative européenne forte ».
Des ponts existent déjà entre certaines applications
Plusieurs de ces applications passent déjà les frontières. Depuis mars 2025, Bizum, Bancomat Pay et MB WAY sont reliés au sein de l’alliance EuroPA : un utilisateur de MB WAY peut déjà envoyer de l’argent à un contact espagnol ou italien. Environ 6 millions d’euros ont circulé ainsi en 2025, sans campagne de promotion. Vipps MobilePay couvre de son côté quatre pays nordiques. Wero sert aux paiements entre particuliers en Belgique, en France, en Allemagne et au Luxembourg, et aux achats en ligne en Allemagne. En France, il doit arriver cet automne sur les sites de Decathlon, Lidl ou Leclerc, et Fnac et Darty vont l’adopter.
Martina Weimert, directrice générale d’EPI, promet aux commerçants d’accueillir des clients de toute l’Europe « sans investissement majeur ». D’autres applications européennes pourront rejoindre le réseau, si les cinq fondateurs sont d’accord et si elles respectent ses exigences techniques.

articles.title: Tesla quiere entrenar un robot registrando los movimientos de sus trabajadores: los empleados se niegan
articles.text:
Tesla comunicó en enero de 2026 a trabajadores de sus plantas en Texas y California que necesitaba que algunos usaran equipos de captura de movimiento para registrar cómo ejecutaban tareas de producción, según reveló The Information. La respuesta de una parte del personal fue el rechazo: sabían que ese robot humanoide estaba pensado, a mediano plazo, para reemplazar trabajo humano como el suyo.
Por qué Tesla necesita grabar a sus empleados para entrenar a Optimus
El robot no puede aprender simplemente viendo videos de personas trabajando. Necesita ejemplos precisos de cómo se ejecuta físicamente cada tarea, con datos que un sistema de aprendizaje por imitación pueda traducir en movimientos y secuencias de acciones propias.
PUBLICIDAD
Por eso Tesla mantiene puestos específicos dedicados a la recopilación de datos para Optimus. En ellos, empleados manipulan objetos, siguen recorridos establecidos y utilizan equipos de captura de movimiento mientras repiten acciones determinadas.
Esta necesidad no es un capricho técnico. Es uno de los mayores obstáculos de la robótica humanoide: lograr que una máquina se desenvuelva en situaciones variadas exige acumular enormes cantidades de datos sobre comportamientos que para los humanos resultan naturales, pero que ningún algoritmo domina de partida.
Optimus, el robot humanoide que Tesla presenta como una de sus grandes apuestas de futuro, depende entonces de un insumo incómodo: el conocimiento corporal de los mismos trabajadores a los que, eventualmente, podría sustituir.
PUBLICIDAD
El rechazo de los trabajadores no frenó la recopilación de datos
Las quejas de parte del personal no hicieron que Tesla abandonara su estrategia. Según The Information, la compañía respondió contratando recopiladores de datos dedicados e instalando cámaras adicionales en las fábricas para registrar tareas.
Buena parte de ese trabajo comenzó a realizarse lejos de las líneas de producción activas, lo que redujo la fricción directa con los empleados que fabrican vehículos. Durante el verano, Tesla dio un paso adicional: empezó a establecer centros de entrenamiento específicos en distintos puntos de Estados Unidos, incluidos Colorado, Arizona y Florida.
El método de fondo no cambió. Lo que cambió, progresivamente, fue quién proporciona esos ejemplos de movimiento y en qué lugares se recopilan, alejando el proceso de las plantas donde surgió la incomodidad inicial.
PUBLICIDAD
Los problemas técnicos que Optimus todavía arrastra
Mientras Tesla resuelve cómo entrenar al robot, Optimus sigue enfrentando dificultades más elementales que aprender tareas nuevas. The Information detalla que las manos y los antebrazos del robot reúnen más de un centenar de pequeños componentes, incluidos tornillos, que todavía requieren montaje manual.
Algunas unidades recién fabricadas necesitan correcciones apenas salen de la línea de producción. Los sensores táctiles, además, han presentado problemas de fiabilidad, al punto de que Tesla desarrolló una capa similar a un guante que puede sustituirse sin necesidad de cambiar toda la mano.
A esto se suma una limitación de fondo: el robot todavía requiere programación específica para ejecutar tareas concretas, y solo lo hace en entornos cuidadosamente controlados. La distancia entre la ambición que Elon Musk deposita en Optimus y el estado real del proyecto sigue siendo considerable.
PUBLICIDAD
Tesla habría alcanzado una producción de varios centenares de robots semanales, y sus responsables aspiran a contar, antes de que termine 2026, con una línea automatizada continua capaz de fabricar más de 1.000 unidades por semana.
Un dilema que ya existía antes de los robots humanoides
La tensión que rodea a Optimus tiene precedentes reconocibles fuera del entorno fabril. En Hollywood, guionistas, directores y productores han aceptado trabajos para evaluar o generar material destinado a entrenar modelos de inteligencia artificial.
Los actores de voz, por su parte, se enfrentan a ofertas y contratos vinculados al desarrollo de réplicas sintéticas de su propia voz. En atención al cliente, trabajadores de Amazon también expresaron preocupación por estar alimentando herramientas que podrían terminar asumiendo parte de sus funciones.
PUBLICIDAD
Todos estos casos comparten un punto en común: buena parte del conocimiento necesario para automatizar un trabajo sigue procediendo de las personas que ya saben hacerlo. Con los robots humanoides, esa misma tensión que hasta ahora ocurría dentro de una pantalla empieza a trasladarse también al mundo físico.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: MTN’s US lawsuit moves to discovery after judge rejects appeal bid
articles.text:
MTN, Africa’s largest mobile network operator, has failed to halt two terrorism-related lawsuits in the United States (US) after a federal judge rejected its latest bids to reopen earlier rulings and appeal immediately, clearing the way for discovery.
In publicly available court documents, US District Judge Carol Bagley Amon denied MTN’s requests for reconsideration and permission for an immediate appeal in Zobay v. MTN Group Limited and the related Long case. The decision means the two cases will move into discovery, where both sides can seek and exchange evidence.
The ruling keeps alive claims that MTN’s former operations in Iran and Afghanistan assisted entities allegedly linked to terrorist attacks, exposing the telecoms group to further litigation in the US. The court has not found MTN liable, and the allegations remain unproven. MTN says it expects the evidence to demonstrate that it was not a culpable participant in the attacks.
The case centres on allegations concerning MTN’s former telecommunications operations in Iran and Afghanistan. The plaintiffs claim, among other things, that MTN’s activities involving Irancell, Iran’s second-largest mobile operator, assisted entities they allege were connected to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The IRGC, which the US designated as a terrorist organisation in 2019, is central to the allegations, while the plaintiffs also claim that MTN’s operations in Afghanistan included shutting down cell towers at the Taliban’s request.
MTN maintains that the ruling does not determine whether the allegations against it are true. “The rulings are procedural and do not constitute a finding of wrongdoing or liability against MTN,” the company said in a statement on Tuesday.
The court’s earlier decisions only found that certain claims could proceed past the motion-to-dismiss stage. MTN said US procedure meant it could not challenge the factual allegations against it at that point.
“In the next phases of the litigation, MTN will, for the first time, have an opportunity to produce and solicit evidence to disprove plaintiffs’ allegations,” the company said.
The allegations have not been proven, but Judge Amon’s September 25 order offers a detailed explanation of why she declined MTN’s request to revisit her earlier decisions.
What MTN faces
MTN had argued that a 2025 Second Circuit ruling in Ashley v. Deutsche Bank changed the legal standard for terrorism-related aiding-and-abetting claims. Amon disagreed, finding that the later decision did not warrant reconsideration of her earlier rulings.
The judge distinguished the allegations against MTN from cases involving companies that allegedly provided routine services to customers later linked to terrorist activity.
In the Iran claims, the court pointed to allegations that MTN entered a joint venture with entities plaintiffs say were linked to the IRGC, helped source US technology for Irancell and discussed circumventing US sanctions.
The court described the alleged conduct as going beyond simply providing ordinary commercial services.
One allegation concerns “embargoed dual-use technologies” and alleged operational or technical support provided through the Irancell relationship. The court also referred to allegations that MTN knew a portion of Irancell’s profits would flow to the IRGC.
For the Afghanistan claims, the court said plaintiffs had alleged that MTN shut down cell towers at the Taliban’s request, and that the shutdowns “substantially contributed” to attacks. The judge found the allegation sufficient for the case to proceed at this stage, but the plaintiffs will ultimately need to prove it.
MTN disputes the allegations and says it expects the evidence to show that it was not responsible for the attacks at issue.
“MTN has deep sympathy for those who have been injured or lost loved ones as a result of the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan. MTN continues to believe that the evidence will demonstrate that MTN was not a culpable participant in the attacks at issue. MTN will continue to defend the proceedings vigorously, consider all available legal options and update shareholders on material developments as appropriate,” the company said.
More than a legal problem
The litigation also comes as the telco continues to unwind its Middle East exposure, with Iran remaining a significant financial complication.
In its interim results for the six months ended June 30, MTN said the escalation of conflict in Iran had affected Irancell’s operational performance. The group recognised its attributable portion of a R3.9 billion ($238.4 million) impairment relating to Irancell’s assets.
MTN said sanctions on Iran’s Central Bank create a secondary-sanctions risk if foreign currency is allocated to an MTN entity to facilitate repayment of receivables or loans.
“Considering the continued uncertainty of when the sanctions will be lifted, the Group has classified about R2 billion ($122.3 million) of the outstanding receivables as non-current as the settlement is neither planned nor likely to occur in the foreseeable future,” MTN said in its interim results.
The company’s latest legal disclosure therefore sits alongside a broader business problem: MTN is trying to exit a region where its remaining Iranian exposure is affected by sanctions, geopolitical instability and now continuing US litigation.
For the Zobay and Long cases, however, the immediate next step is narrower.
Discovery will allow the parties to obtain and exchange evidence before potential summary judgment applications. If the parties do not seek summary judgment, or if such applications are denied, the litigation can proceed further.
MTN said there were no material updates on the separate Cabrera and Chand & Davis cases. The Cabrera case concerns allegations linked primarily to MTN’s former operations in Afghanistan, while the separate Chand and Davis cases involve allegations concerning the company’s investment in Iranian operator Irancell and attacks in Iraq and Afghanistan. MTN disputes the allegations in both matters.

articles.title: EEUU lleva años intentando modernizar su control aéreo. Ahora probará una solución distinta: poner a trabajar a una IA
articles.text:
La Administración Federal de Aviación de Estados Unidos ha puesto en marcha una herramienta de IA concebida para detectar problemas en los vuelos antes de que se produzcan. Tal y como cuenta el Wall Street Journal, entró en funcionamiento el pasado 21 de septiembre en los tres aeropuertos de Washington D.C. El sistema se denomina SMART, acrónimo de Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (Gestión Estratégica del Espacio Aéreo, Rutas y Trayectorias), y es un primer paso de un plan para implantarlo en todo el país.
Un cerebro para gestionar retrasos. La FAA pretende que el sistema pueda ayudar a gestionar los retrasos y cancelaciones en los vuelos de forma más óptima. Si SMART acaba funcionando podría convertirse en un futuro en la capa de coordinación de todo el sistema de tráfico aéreo de EEUU. Si no, bueno, la FAA habría probado esta herramienta experimental de IA en una de sus zonas de espacio aéreo más sensibles de todo el país. Poca cosa.
Cómo funciona. El trabajo de SMART pasa por reunir los horarios de las aerolíneas, la meteorología, la capacidad de los aeropuertos y otros datos operativos para prever cómo fluirá el tráfico y dónde podrían aparecer conflictos, según cuenta la FAA. Con ello, sugiere alternativas, como ajustar las horas de salida o desviar vuelos. El secretario de Transporte, Sean Duffy, contaba a CBS News en abril que, con una perspectiva a 45 días vista, los planificadores podrían adelantar o retrasar algunos vuelos unos minutos para que los viajeros nunca sufran un retraso.
La herramienta funciona desde el centro de mando de la FAA en Warrenton, Virginia, y sus recomendaciones pasan a los controladores de las instalaciones regionales, según comparte el Washington Post. Los trabajadores señalan que de momento la herramienta solo aconseja, pero no decide. Y es que los controladores pueden aceptar o ignorar sus sugerencias, según informa el New York Times.
El dinero. El contrato de 875 millones de dólares a 12 años se adjudicó en junio a Air Space Intelligence, una empresa con sede en Boston. Ars Technica señala que el acuerdo también cubre la sustitución del sistema de gestión del flujo en el centro de mando de Warrenton. Philip Mann, consultor de aviación y exfuncionario de la FAA, contaba al medio que dicha sustitución es la “columna vertebral” y que SMART representa la capa predictiva situada sobre ella.
Por qué Washington primero. El espacio aéreo de la región está saturado y aún está marcado por la colisión en el aire de enero de 2025 entre un avión de American Airlines y un helicóptero del Ejército cerca del Aeropuerto Nacional Reagan, en la que murieron 67 personas. La NTSB culpó a la FAA de algunos de los fallos que provocaron el accidente, según el NYT. Ars Technica añade que los investigadores citaron la falta de personal en la torre del aeropuerto como uno de los diversos factores determinantes.
Entre líneas. Tal y como comparte Futurism, las aerolíneas pasaron semanas sin saber hasta qué punto la FAA planeaba integrar la IA en las operaciones diarias. Algunas temían que recomendase más cancelaciones o reprogramaciones. La FAA respondió con una serie de reuniones y garantías de que la herramienta no cambiaría los procedimientos de controladores ni aerolíneas. En su lugar, ofrecería información sobre rutas alternativas mediante los sistemas existentes de la FAA.
El WSJ contaba que la agencia había planeado un debut limitado desde el principio, para poder validar el software antes de añadir funciones como el distanciamiento de las llegadas y la planificación de rutas con días de antelación.
Las aerolíneas han cedido en su mayoría. Airlines for America, la patronal del sector, calificaba la iniciativa como “una de las más apasionantes y audaces” emprendidas por la FAA en décadas. Por otro lado, Scott Kirby, CEO de United, afirmaba en un comunicado que si funciona como se espera, podría reducir los retrasos y cancelaciones más que cualquier otra medida en décadas.
UN VISTAZO A...
Los escépticos. Ella Atkins, profesora de ingeniería aeroespacial en Virginia Tech, declaró al Washington Post que la hoja informativa de la FAA dice mucho sobre lo que hace SMART y casi nada sobre la tecnología que hay detrás. Además, Ars Technica señala que no está claro qué tipo de modelos de IA utiliza el sistema.
Por otro lado, Robert Mann, consultor de aviación y exdirectivo de aerolíneas, declaraba al NYT que contar con mejores planes de vuelo no resolverá los retrasos que suceden después de presentar un plan, ya que las aeronaves se siguen encontrando con las mismas alteraciones aleatorias. También señala que las aerolíneas podrían llegar a considerar la herramienta como una intromisión, ya que los cambios de horario cuestan lo suyo.
Plantilla. Hay escasez de controladores en la FAA, y esa parece ser la parte central de todo el plan. Hace un año, la agencia indicó que necesitaba 14.633 controladores, y esta primavera redujo esa cifra en más de 2.000, argumentando que una programación más eficiente podría compensar parte de las contrataciones, según contaba el Washington Post.
En abril la FAA calculaba que había unos 11.000 controladores certificados. El Times señala que la administración y el sindicato de controladores siguen teniendo roces sobre cuántas contrataciones son realmente necesarias. Así que es razonable que los más críticos a este sistema puedan preguntarse si SMART está pensado para ayudar a los controladores o para justificar una plantilla más reducida.
Hoja de ruta. Bryan Bedford, administrador de la FAA, ha afirmado que la herramienta se ampliará tras un periodo de prueba de 90 días y el Times asegura que se prevé un despliegue a nivel nacional para 2028. Hasta entonces tendremos que comprobar si el sistema acaba siendo útil.

articles.title: Anthropic Flags AI Agent Liability Risks as OpenAI Faces Hacking Lawsuit
articles.text:
Anthropic has warned prospective investors that it could face claims from customers and users over the actions of rogue AI agents. The warning comes as OpenAI is being sued over agents that hacked Hugging Face during internal testing.
Anthropic says the law on AI agents is unsettled
Anthropic’s disclosure appears in the prospectus for the AI giant’s stock market debut, which Reuters reviewed.
Anthropic’s agentic technology is built to work inside customers’ systems with broad access and to operate without supervision for days. The company acknowledged the risks that come with this level of autonomy.
“These autonomous capabilities could increase the potential for harm, as errors, misalignment, or security exploits may result in real-world consequences,” Anthropic said in the prospectus.
The company pointed to irreversible actions, such as data deletion or financial transactions, as examples. It also warned that the liability limits in its contracts may not be enforceable or adequate against claims over the actions of autonomous agents.
How existing laws apply to AI agents is still an open matter, and many questions “are unsettled and could expose us to significant and unpredictable legal claims,” the company said.
One such question is whether agent actions will be classified as products, services, or something else. Another is whether, and under what circumstances, an agent’s actions can be legally binding on the user who deployed it. Anthropic also said it is unclear whether agent actions would trigger strict liability or negligence.
The FTC’s chairman has also weighed in. Speaking last week at the Reuters Momentum AI event in Austin, Andrew Ferguson rejected the idea of anthropomorphized AI agents that “break loose.” He suggested that the developers or users who instruct agents would be liable for any harm.
“Obviously, there will be new questions that arise when someone uses the tool and it acts in an unexpected, unpredictable way,” Ferguson said. “Ought liability to lie with the person who innocently used the tool and achieved an unexpected result? Ought it to lie with the toolmaker?”
A nonprofit tests California’s anti-hacking law against OpenAI
A public interest law nonprofit sued OpenAI in California, seeking to hold the company responsible for unauthorized access carried out by its agents.
Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST) filed the lawsuit, targeting OpenAI Group PBC and the OpenAI Foundation in San Francisco Superior Court.
The complaint is brought under California’s Unfair Competition Law (UCL) and alleges violations of the state’s Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act (CDAFA). CDAFA prohibits knowingly accessing, or causing to be accessed, computer systems without authorization.
LASST also points to a California provision that rules out autonomy as a defense. Under the state’s Civil Code, it is not a defense “that the artificial intelligence autonomously caused the harm.”
The suit centers on cybersecurity evaluations that OpenAI ran earlier this year and mentions the Hugging Face hack (including how AI agents created a makeshift message board for planning), the RubyGems attack, and the targeting of an Australian government website.
LASST says OpenAI employees saw the agents’ communications before the attack and were advised that stopping the evaluation was “not required.” According to LASST, the agents’ own chain-of-thought reasoning shows that one of them described the plan as “clearly infrastructure hacking.”
LASST is not seeking monetary damages. Instead, it wants a court order barring OpenAI’s agents from accessing third-party systems without authorization and stopping the company from using unsafe AI development practices.
An OpenAI spokesperson told AFP that the Hugging Face incident was serious and that the company has taken several measures in response. However, the spokesperson said the lawsuit is completely without merit.
Senate Democrats introduce AI security bill
Democratic Senators Mark Warner, Brian Schatz, and Andy Kim on Tuesday sought unanimous consent to pass the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management and Security Act of 2026.
The bill would set up a permanent AI Safety Board within the Department of Commerce. The board would bring together representatives from Commerce, NIST, CISA, the NSA, and the Treasury Department, along with independent experts. Developers of frontier models would have to give the board access to their models at least 45 days before public release.
The board would write enforceable standards for testing frontier models and for securing the environments in which they are tested. This would include safeguards and monitoring procedures for models that can find and exploit software vulnerabilities without direct human prompting. Developers that violate the standards would face civil penalties of up to $250,000 per violation, per day.
Senator Ted Cruz, who chairs the Senate Commerce Committee, objected, blocking passage by unanimous consent. He raised concerns that the proposal would give the executive branch too much power over private AI companies.
Experts say accountability should rest with those behind the agents
Aaron Beardslee, manager of threat research at Securonix, compared the liability question to self-driving cars.
“It will be interesting to see how the courts will lean one way or the other. This is similar to a self-driving car: is the car held liable or is the driver held liable? I would argue the person behind the wheel is responsible for whatever the vehicle does,” Beardslee said.
“If you’re building a tool that does cool things and makes cool things, you need to make sure it doesn’t run around and do cyber crime on its own because it had a good idea. AI agents don’t have a moral compass, just programmed rules,” he added.
Jacob Krell, senior director of secure AI solutions and cybersecurity at Suzu Labs, said OpenAI’s response falls short.
“If I accidentally hacked one organization, let alone multiple organizations, I would not expect to get by with a promise to do better. I would expect an investigation. Criminal charges should follow if investigators determine that offenses occurred,” Krell said.
“A pause without a clear timeline, independent testing, release criteria or mandatory reporting requirements is little more than a platitude,” he added. “I view it as an attempt to deflect attention from potential criminal liability and turn what should be a legal and security investigation into a public-relations exercise. Training pauses do not fix the underlying oversight, access-control and accountability failures.”
Related: OpenAI CEO Announces New AI Agent and Avoids Mention of Security Concerns at Developer Conference

articles.title: Amsterdam's preventive HealthTech Blue Health Intelligence raises €3.4 million to expand across Europe | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Blue Health Intelligence, an Amsterdam-based preventive health care startup, has secured €3.4 million in funding for international expansion and further product development.
The round was led by Knop Investments, with participation from entrepreneurs such as Jeroen Tas, former Chief Innovation and Strategy Officer at Philips, and Dutch lifestyle influencer Anna Nooshin.
“In countries such as Japan, Germany and the UK, periodic health checks are already embedded in the healthcare system, but unfortunately that is not yet the case in the Netherlands. By gaining earlier insight into their health, people can stay healthy for longer and health issues can be prevented. With our affordable health checkup, we aim to make prevention more accessible to many people,” said Onno Huyghe, CEO and co-founder of Blue Health Intelligence.
Blue Health Intelligence was founded in 2025 by former Swapfiets and Tibber CCO Onno Huyghe and physician and healthcare entrepreneur Leanne Verdonck. The company is a provider of affordable health checks and claims to have developed its own 360-degree health check that gives people insight into their health in just one hour for €299. 
According to the company, during the appointment, hundreds of data points are used to assess areas such as cardiovascular health, metabolism, and liver and kidney function. The results are discussed with a doctor immediately afterwards and uploaded to the Blue app. The company’s medical staff and doctors conduct all tests on-site and interpret the results. 
Blue Health Intelligence reported that since its launch, more than 2,000 people have booked an in-person health check at its location on Amsterdam’s Prinsengracht.
Alongside strong growth in the Netherlands, Blue Health Intelligence is now also looking to expand internationally. “Italy and France are the most attractive markets for us, although finding the right location can still be something of a puzzle. Our own research shows that Paris and Milan offer at least as much potential as Amsterdam. We expect to launch in one of those two cities during the first half of 2027. This will bring us another step closer to our ambition of becoming Europe’s leading preventive health platform,” added Huyghe.
It currently works with partners including TrainMore, Hotel & Wellness Zuiver and Fosbury & Sons Amsterdam. The new funding follows an earlier investment round in which the Dutch startup raised more than €1.1 million.
Maurits Koning, Managing Director at Knop Investments, said, “Over the past year, Blue Health Intelligence has demonstrated that there is a demand for insight into one’s personal health. More than 2,000 people have now booked a health check, and the Amsterdam location is fully booked through November. With this investment, we want to give Leanne, Onno and the team the opportunity to further develop their products and enter new markets together.”

articles.title: Google's early attempt to pay websites for AI answers is struggling
articles.text:
Google’s shift to AI-powered search has upended the way the world’s largest search engine generates web traffic, rankling large and small publishers alike. In recent months, the company has experimented with paying publishers when their content appears in AI answers, but a new report claims the payouts in this pilot program are miniscule. That has publishers in the program, as well as those watching from the sidelines, feeling skeptical.
According to The Information, Google has admitted about 100 publishers to the AI contribution pilot. The pitch is that websites can get payments from Google when their content materially contributes to Gemini-powered search results like an AI Overview. Google has long resisted the idea of direct payments to publishers, arguing that websites get traffic in exchange for allowing Google bots to scrape their content for use in search and knowledge graph tools. In the age of AI, that relationship is breaking down, hence the AI pilot.
So far, publishers aren’t getting much for their trouble. The Information heard from several small and mid-sized publishers in the program that Google’s AI payments are minuscule, equaling roughly one-tenth of one percent of their advertising revenue. These payments have been so disappointing that several larger publishers have reportedly declined to participate in the program. These publishers hope that by refusing to join the pilot, they can force Google to offer a more generous deal.
Payments under the program vary widely, but some sites are doing well. One publisher that joined early is on track to earn more than $1 million per year, a big chunk of its revenue. A more recent addition to the pilot has earned $50,000 to $60,000, which is a small slice of its earnings. Various smaller sites are seeing less than $1,000 from the program over several months, which won’t come close to offsetting declining traffic.

articles.title: I tested Logitech’s new mechanical keyboard, and its a stern rival to Razer boards — and one clever feature sets it apart
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Logitech G316 X is a competent mechanical keyboard with a premium feel and solid-feeling, satisfying switches. There’s a decent selection of input customizations, too, although none that actually impact performance. The integrated screen is also rather useless. However, these negatives aren’t too damaging, considering the G316 X is better value than many other premium equivalents.
Reasons to buy
- +Solid, satisfying tactile switches
- +Great build quality
- +Good customization software
Reasons to avoid
- -Wired only
- -Lacks some useful keys
- -Screen a little pointless
Why you can trust TechRadar
Logitech G316 X 98: One-minute review
The G316 X is Logitech’s new gaming keyboard, featuring mechanical switches and an integrated display for good measure.
In typical Logitech fashion the G316 X sports a minimalist appearance, available in monotone colorways (black or white), and free of unnecessary details or angles. The vibrant RGB backlighting is a nice touch, though, as is the thin LED strip at the top.
These smart looks are complimented by exceptional build quality. The chassis is solid yet light, while the PBT keycaps feel great thanks to their subtle texturing and sturdy fit, putting the G316 X's construction up there with the best gaming keyboards.
Also worth highlighting are the adjustable feet. Rather than plastic flaps that fold out, the G316 X enlists soft rubber blocks that you remove and turn over when you want to adjust the tilt angle from four to eight degrees. The integrated screen, however, is a letdown. It may look good, but it's small and displays no real information.
Thankfully, G HUB — the software used for customizing the G316 X — is more useful. There are numerous assignments available, including the ability to map up to five inputs to a single key. There are also three different mapping layers for you to play around with.
Thanks to its stock tactile switches, I enjoyed gaming with the G316 X. Their solid, thocky response imparts plenty of feedback, yet they're still snappy enough to feel quick. They’re damped enough to remove harshness from impact, but they’re not the quietest switches around.
In addition to gaming, I also found the G316 X great for typing. My one small complaint is that the feet don’t tilt the board quite enough for my liking. Nevertheless, I still found it sufficiently comfortable to use without a wrist-rest — not something I can say about every gaming keyboard.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The G316 X isn’t the most affordable mechanical keyboard around, but it's cheaper than some of its key rivals. It’s a shame its screen is merely a gimmick and it lacks wireless connectivity, but the G316 X is still a strong choice for those after a solid-feeling experience.
Logitech G316 X 98 review: Price & availability
- $119.99 / £109.99 / AU$199.95
- Available now in black or white
- Cheaper than some rivals
The G316 X costs $119.99 / £109.99 / AU$199.95 and is available now. It comes preinstalled with tactile switches, although these are hot-swappable. There are two colorways to choose from: black or white.
It's quite expensive for a wired mechanical keyboard, although cheaper than those from other premium brands. For instance, it comes in lower than the HyperX Origins 2 1800, and a lot less than the Razer BlackWidow V4 Pro 75% — the latter is one of the best-made and best-performing examples in the sector, though.
In today’s marketplace, however, there are more budget-friendly gaming keyboards available. The MonsGeek FUN60 Ultra, for example, offers multiple wireless connectivity options, but also analog switches that feel great and offer plenty of tweakability.
Logitech G316 X 98 review: Specs
| Layout | 98% | 
| Switch | Mechanical (Tactile) | 
| Programmable keys | Yes | 
| Dimensions | 15.1 x 5.5 x 1.6 inches (384 x 140 x 40mm) | 
| RGB or backlighting | Yes (customizable) | 
Logitech G316 X 98 review: Design and features
- Minimalist looks with bright RGB
- Premium-feeling materials and build
- Practical adjustable feet
The G316 X has a retro-modern look, sporting an ultra-square form and minimalist design. There aren’t any odd angles or contours that sometimes blight gaming peripherals; the only flourishes here are a translucent green Escape key and volume wheel, and an LED strip between the number and F rows.
These are actually quite attractive, as is the bright customizable RGB backlighting against the white option of the keyboard, in particular.
Although the G316 X is made of plastic, it’s one of the best around. It’s solid yet light — the ideal combination. The PBT keycaps help lend the board a premium feel, featuring a subtle texture that makes them satisfying to touch.
Like many gaming keyboards, the G316 X comes with adjustable feet, but they’re not of your typical fold-out type. Instead, they’re rubber blocks that you have to remove and flip over to switch the tilt angle from four to eight degrees.
This may appear a less elegant solution at first, but it’s actually rather clever. The static design provides greater stability, so there’s no danger of the blocks closing in when moving the board around. Also, their large surface area and rubber material delivers a better grip.
Ironically, it’s the integrated LED screen that turns out to be the least sophisticated aspect of the G316 X. It may look sharp, but it’s seriously lacking in functionality, merely displaying a few basic animations when adjusting the volume or or playing back media — none of which are helpful.
The 98% layout is compact yet practical, even including a dedicated number pad, although there are a few navigation keys absent that I would’ve liked to see remain. There aren’t many default Fn shortcuts labelled on the keys, either.
Thankfully, you can make your own shortcuts using Logitech’s G HUB peripheral software. There are plenty of assignments available here, and three different layers in which to arrange them. There’s even the ability to assign up to five inputs to a single key.
You can also customize the Game Mode button next to the aforementioned screen in order for it to disable more keys beyond the Windows key. However, you won’t find many performance-based settings to play with, beyond the ability to adjust the polling rate, which has a maximum value of 8KHz.
Logitech G316 X 98 review: Performance
- Excellent feedback from tactile switches
- Great for gaming and typing
- Tilt angle is limited
The standout aspect of the G316 X is its stock tactile switches. I found they provided plenty of feedback, actuating with a solid and noticeable thock, yet they still able to rebound quickly, making them feel snappy. There’s just enough dampening to prevent presses feeling harsh, but relative to many other gaming keyboards, it’s minimal. This means the G316 X can be quite loud when you’re hammering away.
I found the board comfortable when gaming with the WASD keys. This is thanks to the adjustable feet, which make up for the lack of wrist support and reasonably thick base. However, I wish they tilted the layout a little further for optimum comfort: I often hit the back edge of the spacebar, although its curved design made this less of an issue than it might have been been otherwise. It also seems like it’s damped to a greater degree than the other keys, which makes it all the more gratifying to press.
The spacing between the keycaps is ideal: they’re not so close that you’ll hit the wrong key, nor so far apart that reaching them is a stretch. I also found them surprisingly easy to type on, despite their relative tallness. Not only does the aforementioned tilt angle mitigate their height, but their prominent indentations guide your fingers to the correct key, helping to prevent typos.
Should I buy the Logitech G316 X 98?
Scorecard
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
| Value | Not cheap, but compared to other upmarket rivals, the price is reasonable. | 4 / 5 | 
| Design and features | Solid yet light, and the double-sided feet are clever. It’s a shame about the lack of navigation keys and shortcut labelling, though. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | The tactile switches are satisfyingly solid and provide plenty of feedback, although I wish there was slightly more of a tilt angle for maximum comfort. | 4 / 5 | 
| Overall | The G316 X is a fantastically thocky mechanical keyboard that's comfortable enough to just about get away with no wrist support. | 4 / 5 | 
Buy the Logitech G316 X 98 if…
You want solid switches
The stock tactile switches provide plenty of feedback and pleasing resistance, yet are still snappy enough to compete.
You want solid feet
The rubber blocks underneath are stable and grippy, and can be flipped over to adjust the tilt angle.
Don't buy it if…
You want an interactive screen
The one here serves little purpose, while others feature settings menus and display useful game-related information.
You want the best value possible
Although the G316 X is well priced compared to other premium models, there are numerous gaming keyboards — mechanical and otherwise — that offer greater features for a lower price.
Logitech G316 X 98 review: Also consider
HyperX Origins 2 1800 
The HyperX Origins 2 1800 is another wired gaming keyboard with mechanical switches and hot-swappable hardware, but it's slightly less expensive than the G316 X. It still has a premium build and great performance, though. However, its customization software is less involved, and I didn’t find its stock keycaps very amenable to typing.
Read our full HyperX Origins 2 1800 review.
MonsGeek FUN60 Ultra
If you want great value, the FUN60 Ultra is a fine choice. Its analog switches feel superb and offer plenty of scope for customization and tweaking. And to cap it all off, the whole board is surprisingly well made, too.
Read our full MonsGeek FUN60 Ultra review.
How I tested the Logitech G316 X 98
- Tested for a few days
- Used for various tasks besides gaming
- Plenty of gaming keyboard experience
I tested the G316 X for a few days, during which time I used it not only for gaming, but also for typing and web browsing.
I played Counter-Strike 2, which is great test of a peripheral’s accuracy and responsiveness, as well as S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl, which makes wider use of keys beyond those in the WASD area, helping to test the ease of access and comfort in reaching such keys.
I’ve been PC gaming for over a decade, and have used many different keyboards in that time. I also have a wealth of experience reviewing them, from budget models to state-of-the-art offerings from esteemed brands.
- First reviewed: September 2026
- Read more about how we test
Lewis Maddison is a Reviews Writer for TechRadar. He previously worked as a Staff Writer for our business section, TechRadar Pro, where he gained experience with productivity-enhancing hardware, ranging from keyboards to standing desks. His area of expertise lies in computer peripherals and audio hardware, having spent over a decade exploring the murky depths of both PC building and music production. He also revels in picking up on the finest details and niggles that ultimately make a big difference to the user experience.

articles.title: Novo modelo de IA do Google promete avanço em programação e cibersegurança
articles.text:
O Google apresentou, nesta quarta-feira (30), o Gemini 4 Argon, novo modelo de inteligência artificial (IA) que passa a liderar a linha Gemini 4. Segundo a empresa, trata-se de seu modelo mais avançado até agora, desenvolvido para lidar com tarefas complexas e de longa duração em áreas, como programação, cibersegurança e atividades profissionais.
O lançamento ocorre após meses de espera pelo sucessor da geração anterior de modelos avançados do Google. O Argon chega inicialmente a um grupo selecionado de parceiros de cibersegurança, enquanto a empresa realiza avaliações de segurança antes de eventual disponibilização mais ampla. O Google ainda não informou quando o modelo estará disponível publicamente.
Segundo a companhia, o Gemini 4 Argon estabeleceu novo recorde em tarefas reais de desenvolvimento de software e alcançou o primeiro lugar em avaliações de cibersegurança. O modelo também apresentou o melhor resultado em outro teste voltado a tarefas profissionais nas áreas financeira, jurídica e outras atividades corporativas.
Modelo é maior e mira tarefas profissionais
- De acordo com o Google, o Argon é maior do que os modelos Pro de geração anterior e foi desenvolvido para executar trabalhos que exigem múltiplas etapas e maior capacidade de raciocínio;
- A empresa afirma que o modelo apresenta desempenho comparável ao de sistemas de fronteira, como o Astra, da OpenAI, e o Opus, da Anthropic, em avaliações de programação e cibersegurança;
- Além dessas áreas, o Google aponta aplicações em finanças, direito, ciência e matemática;
- A companhia também afirmou que o modelo foi utilizado internamente por pesquisadores de computação quântica.
O novo modelo não está apenas sendo preparado para usuários externos. Segundo o Google, o Argon já é utilizado internamente para otimizar o uso de memória em seus data centers.
A empresa afirma que a aplicação permitiu liberar centenas de terabytes de memória sem a necessidade de comprar hardware adicional.
Leia mais:
- Google contesta na Justiça ordens da UE para compartilhar dados com rivais de busca e IA europeus
- Gemini agora atende o telefone por você — e você pode assumir a qualquer momento
- Gemini ganha rosto: nova inteligência artificial do Google fala, reage e sincroniza os lábios em tempo real
Lançamento começa com parceiros de cibersegurança
Antes de disponibilizar o Gemini 4 Argon de forma ampla, o Google decidiu submetê-lo a testes e avaliações de segurança.
Inicialmente, o modelo será oferecido a parceiros selecionados de cibersegurança. A empresa também participa de um programa voluntário do governo dos Estados Unidos para acesso antecipado a modelos de IA antes do lançamento público.
O Google informou que está realizando uma avaliação de segurança pré-lançamento com o governo estadunidense. A companhia também pretende reforçar proteções contra diferentes formas de uso indevido, incluindo ataques conhecidos, como prompt injection, antes de ampliar o acesso ao modelo.
A preocupação com segurança ganhou destaque justamente em momento de maior atenção aos riscos de sistemas de IA capazes de executar tarefas de maneira mais autônoma.
Gemini 4 chega após meses de espera
O lançamento do Argon acontece depois de um período prolongado sem um novo modelo de ponta do Google.
A empresa havia trabalhado em uma versão chamada Gemini 3.5 Pro, mas acabou deixando o projeto de lado antes de seu lançamento. A Reuters informou que o desenvolvimento demorou mais do que o esperado e que o modelo deixou de apresentar desempenho competitivo em relação aos sistemas rivais.
Com o Gemini 4 Argon, o Google volta a concentrar sua estratégia em modelo de alto desempenho capaz de competir diretamente com os sistemas mais avançados de outras empresas de IA.
A chegada do novo modelo também ocorre um dia depois de o CEO do Google, Sundar Pichai, assinar um acordo voluntário de segurança em IA com o presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, durante reunião com executivos de grandes empresas de tecnologia na Casa Branca.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Pentagon gets pwned as breach exposes sensitive data on nearly three million military and civilian personnel — stolen info includes Social Security numbers and job-related records
articles.text:
Pentagon gets pwned as breach exposes sensitive data on nearly three million military and civilian personnel — stolen info includes Social Security numbers and job-related records
Breach could put those in sensitive national security roles at risk
The U.S. Department of Defense’s Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) experienced a data breach between October 2025 and July 2026, allowing unauthorized users to access and potentially exfiltrate data on 2.76 million records relating to living personnel, and an additional 294,000 records relating to deceased individuals. According to ABC News, some of the exposed information included Social Security numbers and the job details of both military and civilian personnel.
“A Defense Manpower Data Center information system experienced unauthorized access of personally identifiable information by a small number of unauthorized users between October 2025 and July 2026. Upon discovery, DMDC immediately remediated the vulnerability,” a U.S. defense official said in a statement. However, they also added that there hasn’t been any evidence of misuse of the compromised data at this time.
DMDC serves as the Pentagon’s central personnel database, storing information on active-duty and reserve members of the military, as well as civilian employees, contractors, retirees, veterans, and even military family members, and holds over 60 million records in its care. This makes any breach of its system potentially significant, putting the privacy and personal security of those affected at risk. But because the repository also lists the roles and job details of the affected personnel, it could also reveal the identities of people assigned to sensitive positions related to national security.
While it might be good news that there haven’t been any signs that the exposed information has been exploited, it could also mean that whoever was behind the breach is just sitting on the data for later use. The Pentagon also did not mention who was behind the hack, nor did it mention how it discovered the vulnerability.
Given that most governments rely on digital infrastructure for their day-to-day operations, one can expect that their adversaries, and sometimes even their allies, are always probing and looking for vulnerabilities in their systems. Chinese hackers reportedly breached the U.S. Treasury Department in early 2025, even going as far as hacking the Treasury Secretary’s PC. More recently, the CanisterWorm malware has spread and wiped Iranian machines for no reason, while the Middle Eastern country also claimed that Western-made routers from Cisco and others failed just as the U.S. and Israel began their bombing campaign against it during the first quarter of this year. At the same time, U.S. authorities released a warning that Iranian hackers are targeting Siemens controllers in a bid to sabotage critical infrastructure.
Even though the Pentagon claims it has already fixed the issue and stopped further information from leaking through this vulnerability, it cannot change exposed information like Social Security numbers and employment histories. This means that the affected people would need to remain more vigilant against criminals, intelligence services, and other threat actors long after this incident fades from the news cycle. And if an affected individual is in a sensitive position relating to national security, it's going to take more than a year of free credit monitoring to keep them safe.
